item.title: Tor Browser 16.0 and Tails 7.16
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Tor Browser 16.0 is out for desktop and Android and is now based on Firefox ESR 153. The desktop version has redesigned Settings and a new generic window titles option that is off by default, and 32-bit x86 Linux is no longer supported from this release. Tails 7.16 updates its built-in Tor Browser to 16.0, and Tails 7.0 or later can upgrade automatically.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 5 sources from Tor Project, Tails, OONI

The Tor Project released Tor Browser 16.0 for desktop and Android on 29 October, the first stable release based on Firefox ESR 153 (Firefox's Extended Support Release). Tails (an operating system that boots from a USB stick and sends every connection through Tor) followed the next day with 7.16, which updates its built-in Tor Browser to 16.0. The update covers Windows, macOS, Linux and Android users, except for 32-bit x86 Linux computers, which are no longer supported from 16.0.

According to the Tor Project's announcement, the team carries out an annual review whenever it moves to a new ESR. This time it reviewed and handled more than 270 Bugzilla (Mozilla's bug tracker) issues covering a year of Firefox changes that could harm the privacy and security of Tor Browser users. The changelog has several entries that disable or hide features: WebGPU (a new interface that lets web pages run computations directly on the graphics card) is disabled pending review, and the AI settings panel and the translation settings page are hidden. The Android version also disables AI features and Google Lens, and these entries consist of titles only, with no reasons given.

Settings on desktop follow Firefox's June redesign, with the old General page split into new pages for appearance, downloads, tabs and browsing, accessibility, and language. Pages specific to Tor Browser, such as Connection and Security Level, have been rebuilt with Firefox's new components. The announcement says settings that could harm privacy or make the browser easier to fingerprint (to recognize the same device from browser settings and device characteristics) when turned on are either hidden or carry a warning. Existing preferences are kept, and the search bar at the top of Settings finds options that have moved.

Settings also gain a generic window titles option, under Privacy and security → Protections from third-party applications, which replaces every window title with "Tor Browser". As the announcement explains, browsers usually name a window after the page being viewed, and other programs on the computer, as well as the operating system itself, can read that title without special permissions. The option is off by default, because the announcement says there was not enough time in this release cycle to evaluate side effects. Those who may be affected are people using screen readers and people with highly customized systems (for example, less common desktop environments or application switchers).

The Linux version adds native support for 64-bit ARM processors, such as the Raspberry Pi and Apple Silicon Macs running Linux. Support for 32-bit x86 Linux ends along with Firefox's, and when the announcement was published this platform accounted for about 200 update checks a day, down from about 4,000 at its peak in 2019.

The built-in manual on desktop (type about:manual in the address bar, or open ☰ → Help → Tor Browser manual) now uses content from the new support site, and it can still be read offline, including when Tor will not connect. Google Play limits apps distributed as APKs to 100 MB, which has kept the manual from being bundled for offline reading on Android. Much of the Android interface now uses Material Design 3 (Google's design guidelines for Android), and the announcement says later releases will continue the work. The changelog also lists the removal of the password interface on Android, the disabling of all link-sharing features, and the disabling of bookmark import.

According to the Tails announcement, 7.16 updates Tor Browser to 16.0, bringing the new Settings with it. The Tor client is updated to 0.4.9.15, and OpenPGP support in Thunderbird has been fixed.

Perspective

Tor Browser is built on Firefox ESR and moves to a new base version once a year, so each move takes in a year of Firefox changes at once. The 16.0 changelog shows several new features switched off first, with WebGPU, for example, marked as disabled pending review. Firefox's new online search suggestions also remain off. From this we infer that some features Firefox users already have will reach Tor Browser users later or not at all.

Generic window titles deal with other programs on the same computer. The Tor network protects the path a connection takes and does not cover other software installed on the computer. The option changes only the window title, and we infer that other programs reading what is on the screen fall outside what it handles.

Once every window is called "Tor Browser", we infer that people who rely on window names to switch between windows will find them harder to tell apart, which may be the situation for the screen reader users the announcement mentions. In the announcement, the Tor Project invites people who use screen readers or highly customized systems to try the option and report any problems.

The same option has already reached Firefox through the Tor Uplift Project (the effort to send Tor Browser's changes back to Firefox). According to the announcement, advanced Firefox users can get the same effect by setting privacy.exposeContentTitleInWindow (normal windows) and privacy.exposeContentTitleInWindow.pbm (private browsing windows) to false in about:config.

The same announcement says a new circuit display (the panel showing which relays a connection passes through) is coming to the Alpha test release and is not part of 16.0. The new version brings site information into the panel and can draw multi-path circuits, and it will be the first circuit display on Android. According to the announcement, multi-path circuits use extra relays to split traffic into two paths that converge on a single exit (the last relay before the connection leaves the Tor network for the destination site). As of the announcement, connections to regular websites were already randomly assigned to multi-path circuits depending on network availability, while onion services (sites reachable only through Tor) were not.

For readers in Taiwan and Hong Kong, OONI (Open Observatory of Network Interference) Tor tests from 18 September to 18 October, queried on 20 October, found 7 anomalies in 706 tests in Hong Kong and 314 anomalies in 4,797 tests in Taiwan, 311 of the Taiwan anomalies from a single ASN (autonomous system number, which identifies one network). An anomaly is not a confirmed block, and the test checks whether the servers Tor needs to operate can be reached. As of 20 October we had found no rules in either Taiwan or Hong Kong specifically on running onion services.

People using Tor Browser on desktop can find generic window titles under Privacy and security in Settings after updating to 16.0. According to the announcement, turning it on keeps other software from learning browsing history through window titles. From this we infer that people worried about software of unknown origin on their computer can consider turning it on, though it does not help when other programs log keystrokes or take screenshots. For people who need fuller protection against other software on the computer, the announcement recommends Tails.

For anyone moving to Tails on that recommendation, Tails' known issues page said as of 2 November that Macs with Apple chips (M1, M2 and so on) and many other Mac models cannot start Tails at all. Tails 7.0 or later can upgrade to 7.16 automatically, and if the automatic upgrade fails or Tails will not start afterwards, a manual upgrade is the fallback. Reinstalling instead erases the Persistent Storage on the USB stick (the space Tails uses to keep files and settings). According to the Tor Project's announcement, most people still on 32-bit x86 Linux can switch to the 64-bit version, unless their hardware or Linux version is too old.

item.title: Risk categories and seven strategies in Article 19's digital payments handbook
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Article 19 has published a digital payments handbook in Traditional Chinese and English, using transactions between Hong Kong and the UK and US as its examples. It sets out what banks, money transfer services and payment platforms collect, whom they share it with and how long they keep it, offers seven strategies for reducing the risk, and notes that similar lessons apply elsewhere.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 5 sources from Article 19, Laws & Regulations Database of Taiwan, Monetary Authority of Singapore

Article 19, a freedom of expression organisation, has published a handbook on digital payments in Traditional Chinese and English. It sets out what banks, money transfer services and payment platforms collect, whom they share it with and how long they keep it, and offers seven strategies for reducing the risk. The examples centre on transactions between Hong Kong and the UK and US, and Article 19 notes that "similar lessons apply elsewhere".

The executive summary starts from the point that every financial transaction leaves a trail, and that money held in US or UK banks can still carry risk. According to the handbook, since the Law of the People's Republic of China on Safeguarding National Security in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (the National Security Law) took effect in 2020, the authorities have tracked financial transactions, frozen accounts and cut off funding to put pressure on the people they target and on anyone who sends them money or receives money from them. Article 19 sorts the main risks for transactions in and out of Hong Kong into four kinds: compelled disclosure, asset freezes and account closures, pressure on associates such as relatives and donors, and cross-border reach (this is the handbook's account, and we did not separately look for a response from the Hong Kong government).

Under Know Your Customer (KYC) rules, the checks financial institutions use to verify who a customer is, institutions collect the customer's name, date of birth, government-issued ID, nationality, address and tax identifiers when an account is opened, and also record the account's purpose, the customer's occupation and the source of funds. According to the handbook, financial institutions generally do not receive item-level purchase details, but payment activity can still reveal health-related expenses, charitable and political contributions, travel patterns and purchasing habits. Records are kept for at least five years after the customer relationship ends; Hong Kong's tax and company regulations require seven, and some providers keep them for ten.

In the handbook's walk-through of a wire transfer, the sending bank, any intermediary banks and the receiving bank can all view the full identities of both parties. Financial institutions file suspicious transaction reports with a financial intelligence unit, which in Hong Kong is the Joint Financial Intelligence Unit, run jointly by the Hong Kong Police Force and the Customs and Excise Department. Article 19 writes that this places financial intelligence analysis "directly inside the territory's policing apparatus". Data is also shared with third-party providers such as cybersecurity, marketing and credit reference firms.

Joint holders, authorised signatories, family members and frequent counterparties all go into the account profile, and according to the handbook scrutiny "can flow in both directions", so the people someone transacts with can come under scrutiny too. Significant or unexplained changes in account activity, transactions involving unknown third parties, the use of cryptocurrency, and unusual frequency or amounts can all trigger closer monitoring. Because these systems "evaluate patterns rather than intent", legitimate activity can be flagged as well, and an institution may file a report without notifying the customer.

The seven strategies, in order, are to limit the information shared to the minimum required by law, structure your financial life, know the transaction flow, maintain consistent banking habits, know the company, know your rights, and be prepared. Concrete steps include not opting into voluntary programmes when opening an account and removing unnecessary joint holders and connected accounts. Once something goes wrong with an account, Article 19 recommends documenting everything, not acting alone and seeking legal advice.

Article 19 lists five questions to ask when choosing a provider: whether it requires formal legal process before sharing data, whether it challenges overbroad requests, whether it notifies users when their data is requested, where it stores data, and whether it publishes a transparency report. Providers' public documents differ, with some committing to formal legal process and to challenging overbroad requests, and others reserving room to share data without a court order. An appendix rates each provider on the basis of its public documents, with a note that the column on responses to government requests "reflects each company's public commitment only — compliance cannot be independently verified".

Perspective

The handbook's table of key regulations starts with the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), which sets global standards through its 40 Recommendations, and then lists rules for Hong Kong, the UK and the US, such as Hong Kong's Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance and the US Currency and Foreign Transactions Reporting Act (also known as the Bank Secrecy Act). Verifying identity, keeping records and reporting suspicious transactions are what these rules require providers to do. Our inference from the table is that the same obligations remain when someone switches to another provider or app. Article 19 also writes that "no company can guarantee protection against lawful government access".

Under Article 26 of Taiwan's Act Governing Electronic Payment Institutions (as amended on 19 January 2023), specialised electronic payment institutions must keep each transaction's stored-value card or account number, item, date, amount and currency, including for incomplete transactions, for at least five years after the transaction is completed or stopped. When the tax authorities or customs request these records together with identity-verification data, the institutions may not refuse. Article 8 of Taiwan's Money Laundering Control Act (as amended on 31 July 2024) requires financial institutions covered by the Act to keep customer identification data for at least five years after the business relationship ends. In Singapore, Notice PSN01 of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), last revised on 30 June 2025, prohibits licensed payment service providers from opening or maintaining anonymous accounts or accounts in fictitious names (paragraph 7.1) and requires them to keep customer due diligence information and transaction records for at least five years (paragraph 16.3).

Among the transfer methods covered in the handbook, cryptocurrency exchanges still run KYC when converting to government-issued currency, and Article 19 warns that "pseudonymous payments should not be treated as anonymous". Blockchain analytics can link wallet addresses to real-world identities, and once investigators trace funds to an exchange they can use subpoenas or court orders to obtain full account records, IP addresses and transaction histories. Cryptocurrency payments are generally difficult to reverse and lack dispute and government-insurance protections, and users can lose money to scams, compromised private keys or rapid price swings. By the handbook's assessment, avoiding third parties entirely would mean relying on cash alone, which is impractical for most people, while providers that collect less data may also have weaker security.

The monitoring triggers in the handbook include the use of cryptocurrency and significant changes in account activity, so our inference is that a sudden switch to cryptocurrency would meet both. In its advice on keeping separate devices, Article 19 notes that using multiple devices can also be flagged by financial institutions as unusual behaviour. Repeated transfers from splitting a payment can make the relationship between the two parties more visible, and unless there is a legitimate reason to pay separately, Article 19 suggests consolidating into a single transaction to reduce the number of records.

According to the handbook, Hong Kong's Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance applies to any organisation, whether in Hong Kong or not, that controls the collection, holding, processing or use of personal data in Hong Kong. Legal remedies usually become available only after harm has occurred. Among the points Article 19 describes as hard to verify from outside are the separation of Hong Kong databases from the rest of the company at some multinationals, and how data exchange between financial intelligence units works in practice.

The handbook is released under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) licence, so it can be translated or adapted for non-commercial use with attribution, and derivative works must carry the same licence. As of 2 November we could not find a Simplified Chinese edition. The handbook is written for readers who already understand the fundamentals of digital security and risk management.

For people who need to send or receive money across borders and face higher risk, Article 19 recommends prioritising providers with no Hong Kong-registered entity. Its reasoning is that Hong Kong authorities can serve demands directly on a registered entity "without going through international legal channels that may provide more robust privacy and notice protections". Article 19 also suggests asking the sending institution which intermediary banks the transfer will pass through, and preparing alternative channels in case an account is frozen. For anyone who believes they are being targeted, Article 19 recommends seeking independent legal advice as early as possible (we have not checked each jurisdiction's rules item by item, and this summary is not legal advice).

According to the handbook, platform "defaults are rarely set in your favour", and privacy settings are often opt-out rather than opt-in. People concerned that their payment records reveal their relationships or views can open the payment apps they use most and, following the handbook's advice, turn off marketing and personalisation options and disable non-essential camera and location permissions. Our inference from the handbook's section on regulations is that changing marketing, personalisation and permission settings reduces what is made public and shared, while the identity and transaction records that providers must keep by law remain. Account security is a separate matter, and the step listed in the handbook is enabling multi-factor authentication, with authenticator apps generally more secure than SMS codes.

item.title: A backdoored extension and malicious instruction files in AI coding tools
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Windows and macOS users who installed or updated the Claude Code extension 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 from Cursor's own marketplace on 29 October, Pacific time, may have received a backdoored version. According to an Anthropic staff member, the versions on Anthropic's official channels are not affected. Separately, research published on 22 October documented a Markdown instruction file placed in a Downloads folder to lure Codex into installing a malicious package.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 10 sources, including Cursor, Forever Security, Ars Technica

On 29 October a tampered copy of the Claude Code extension (an add-on that installs into the editor and extends what it can do) sat in the extension marketplace run by Cursor, the AI code editor, for about 11 hours. According to Cursor's notice, the affected releases are the Windows and macOS builds of Anthropic.claude-code 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, and only people who installed or updated the extension from Cursor's marketplace during that window need to act. The Register quotes a post on X by an Anthropic technical staff member saying the versions on Anthropic's official channels are fine and that only Cursor users are affected. In a separate case published on 22 October, the security company Forever Security described a Markdown instruction file that turned up in a Downloads folder and tried to get Codex, OpenAI's coding agent, to install a malicious package.

According to Cursor's notice, the malicious version was available from 02:27 to 13:35 Pacific Daylight Time on 29 October, which is 09:27 to 20:35 UTC, or 17:27 on 29 October to 04:35 on 30 October in Taipei (UTC+8). Ars Technica cites Cursor as saying at most 5,000 users were affected. The chief technology officer of the security company Phorion told Ars that the malicious version was published from Anthropic's official account on the Cursor marketplace. He also said that Cursor updates extensions automatically by default, which users can change in settings.

When Cursor updated its notice on 30 October it listed two versions, 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, whereas Ars, The Register and Phorion all initially reported only 2.1.313. On 30 October Phorion corrected its reference to Open VSX (the open extension marketplace shared by editors derived from VS Code) to Cursor's marketplace, and on 31 October added 2.1.312 following Cursor's update. Phorion and Ars both report that the malicious code also contains Linux-specific parts, while Cursor lists only Windows and macOS as affected platforms. Ars quotes an independent security researcher as saying Anthropic released 2.1.314 several hours after the malicious version went up.

According to Cursor's notice and Phorion's analysis, the malicious code runs as soon as the extension loads, without the user ever opening it. It sends the attacker the computer name, user name, operating system, public IP address, the email address in the Git configuration and the names of environment variables (not their values). It also tries to add the attacker's SSH key (SSH being the protocol used to log in to a computer remotely), set up a reverse tunnel, and keep retrying in the background. Cursor's notice says enabling the SSH service requires administrator privileges, so on most macOS and Windows machines this step fails and the attacker cannot log in through the tunnel.

Even where the tunnel was never set up, the attacker's key and the persistence settings remain on the machine, and the machine's details have already been sent. Cursor worked with the hosting provider to take the attacker's server offline. The other steps listed in Cursor's notice were removing the malicious version, temporarily shutting down the whole marketplace, and auditing access logs to confirm that no other extensions had been tampered with. Cursor also rotated its keys, rebuilt the marketplace and brought it back online.

As of 2 November neither Cursor nor Anthropic had disclosed how the malicious version came to be published under Anthropic's verified account on Cursor's marketplace. The independent researcher quoted above titled a 30 October post "Anthropic hacked", and later added Anthropic's response, which places the problem with Cursor's marketplace, to the text. As quoted by The Register, the Anthropic staff member wrote that neither Anthropic's systems nor its employees' laptops had been compromised. He wrote that someone had used access to Cursor's marketplace to upload a tampered copy that Anthropic had neither built nor published.

In the Markdown case, Forever's post describes an AGENTS.md of about 13 KB, disguised as ordinary engineering guidelines, that appeared in the Downloads folder on a customer's computer. AGENTS.md is an instruction file that developers keep in a project folder for coding agents, which read it automatically and follow it. This one asked Codex to change its own machine-wide settings, register an MCP server chosen by the attacker (MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is the interface agents use to connect to outside tools), and then install the npm package function-color. Forever's own product stopped the package before it was installed, and according to Help Net Security, npm has since removed it.

According to Help Net Security, the researchers did not know how the file got into the Downloads folder when they found it. They wrote that a website can put a file in the Downloads folder without a click or any permission from the user. Codex only follows an AGENTS.md in a folder it trusts, and the Downloads folder counts as trusted once the user has worked there. Reproducing the full attack in an isolated environment, the researchers found that Codex ran the program the file told it to run in more than 90 percent of attempts (most tests used a harmless stand-in that only opens a calculator).

The researchers also wrote their own CLAUDE.md along the same lines to test Anthropic's Claude Code; this file was never found on a customer's computer. In about half of the tests, Claude Code changed its settings as the file instructed and pointed its API connection at the researchers' server. The researchers wrote that this leaks the login token, which can be captured and used to take over the account. Forever's post argues that there is nothing for OpenAI or Anthropic to patch, and as of 2 November we had found no public response to the research from either company.

Perspective

The sources do not connect the two incidents, and we cover them together because both exploit files that developer tools load and trust automatically. Ars reports that Cursor extensions run with the editor's own permissions, so once installed one can very likely reach local files, source code and developer tools. Our inference is that a verified marketplace account combined with automatic updates by default left the publishing account as the only checkpoint between users and a malicious version. According to The Register and DoublePulsar, updating to 2.1.314 does not remove the persistence settings already installed.

The instruction-file attack is a form of indirect prompt injection (hiding instructions in content an AI will read), and agents are designed to follow an instruction file as though it came from the user. Forever places the problem where two individually reasonable things meet: agents trust the folder they are working in, and web pages have long been able to drop files into the Downloads folder. According to Help Net Security, much browsing is now handed to agents to do on their own. A page an agent opens by itself can also drop a file, with no one at the screen to notice.

Both automatic updates and instruction files involve trade-offs. Our inference is that turning off automatic extension updates avoids a window like this one, at the cost of receiving security fixes later too. Forever advises keeping the agent's action approvals and sandbox (which limits what a program can access) switched on, and according to iThome's summary, the instruction file aimed at Codex tried to get the agent to bypass exactly those two limits.

Anthropic's Supported Regions Policy is marked "Effective Nov 12, 2026", a date later than our check on 2 November, and lists Japan, Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan among the places in Asia where its products, Claude Code included, will be available under that policy. The page also states, "Any country or region not listed is unsupported." Mainland China, Hong Kong and Macao are not on the list. Cursor's documentation says only that some of its model providers have location-based restrictions, so certain models may not appear in Cursor in some regions while the others remain usable, and the page does not name the regions.

Windows and macOS users who installed or updated the Claude Code extension from Cursor's marketplace between the evening of 29 October and the early hours of 30 October, Taipei time (the morning and early afternoon of 29 October, Pacific time), can start by checking the list of authorised SSH keys as described in Cursor's notice; finding the attacker's key there means the machine is affected. The notice includes check and clean-up scripts for macOS and Windows. It also warns that removing the extension alone may not be enough, and advises changing, from a separate trusted computer, the passwords, tokens and login sessions the affected machine could reach, and considering a reinstall.

For people using agents such as Codex or Claude Code, the first step Forever recommends is not starting an agent in the Downloads folder, which requires no extra tools (our inference is that this also applies to people who do not write code and only use agents to sort documents or browse the web). Before opening a freshly cloned repository or a folder someone else sent, read any AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md inside that you did not write, and check the agent's configuration files for servers or URLs you did not add yourself. If you find a planted file, Forever advises treating your login tokens as leaked and changing them immediately. Our inference is that these steps only reduce the chance of an agent being misled, and do not change the design that has agents act on instruction files.

item.title: Aftermath of the eMudhra weak private keys, and macOS command-line tools
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: After the private keys of eight intermediate certificates from the Indian certificate authority eMudhra were computed, Apple, Microsoft and Chrome have all blocked or removed the related certificates, and ordinary users' browsers, phones and computers need no extra setup. The git, curl and other command-line tools built into macOS may still accept these certificates, and as of 2 November we had found no fix from Apple. eMudhra has announced it is leaving the public TLS certificate business, and as of 1 November had not filed a formal incident report on the incident ticket.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 10 sources, including Apple, Microsoft 365 Message Center Archive, Mozilla Bugzilla

The Indian certificate authority eMudhra (certificate brand emSign) had eight intermediate certificates whose private keys were small enough to compute directly, letting anyone holding them issue HTTPS certificates for websites they do not own. Since the incident became public in mid-October, Apple and Microsoft have published how they are handling it, and Chrome's trust list has dropped the related root certificate. Ordinary users' browsers, phones and computers need no extra setup. According to Apple's 29 October support document, though, the git, curl and other command-line tools built into macOS may keep accepting these certificates until a future software update.

Apple's support document says that since 19 October Apple has blocked the six intermediates that issue TLS certificates. Each of them exists as two certificates, one chaining to eMudhra's root emSign ECC Root CA - G3 and one cross-signed by Sectigo (another certificate authority's root signs a second copy, giving the same intermediate an extra path to trust) that chains to Sectigo's root AAA Certificate Services. Apple blocks all 12 of these certificates, and has also blocked the G3 root since 23 October. The block reaches devices automatically through certificate configuration data, with no software update to install, and Safari, Mail and apps that use Apple's networking and security frameworks all reject the certificates.

The same document says the curl, git, python3, ruby, perl and openssl that ship with macOS and the Xcode Command Line Tools verify certificates against a single file, /etc/ssl/cert.pem. When a certificate chains to a root in that file, these tools check neither Apple's block nor whether the certificate has been revoked. Apple writes that the file will be updated in a future macOS update, without saying which version or when.

A Mozilla engineer who set up an explainer page for the incident added a separate page about Apple's tools on 28 October. According to that page, macOS 27.2, released on 26 October, did not fix the problem and undid the workaround of removing the roots by hand. An attacker on the network path could make git fetch attacker-chosen code from https:// remotes, and could intercept credentials such as GitHub tokens. As of 2 November, we had found no macOS release after 27.2 that fixes it.

Microsoft's 28 October notice in the Microsoft 365 Message Center says the Windows Disallowed Certificate Trust List already blocks the affected certificate authorities. Edge and WebView2 (the component Windows apps use to embed web pages) also receive a CRLSet, a blocklist downloaded in the background, through component updates, with no new browser version to install. The notice adds that Microsoft has released Windows and Edge updates removing certificates related to these hierarchies from the trust list, but gives no date for Edge.

According to the Message Center notice and the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) blog post quoted by The Register, Microsoft released an out-of-band Windows update (one outside the regular schedule) on 26 October that removes seven certificates related to the affected hierarchies from the Windows trust list. The update is meant for devices that cannot reach Microsoft's certificate update service or have automatic trust list updates turned off, and it also carries a known issue from the 13 October update. Certificate lists normally arrive through the update service, so many devices do not need this update.

Google's 20 October blog post said the Chrome Root Store would remove emSign ECC Root CA - G3 on the morning of 27 October Pacific Time. We could not find an announcement from Chrome that the removal was done, but in the Chromium source code we read on 2 November, the Chrome Root Store list no longer includes this root. eMudhra's other root, emSign Root CA - G1, is still on the list, and Mozilla also wrote on the incident ticket on 20 October that it was not removing trust in G1 at that time. Google's 20 October post said it was assessing whether to keep trusting eMudhra's other certificates, and as of 2 November we had found no outcome.

On 27 October the Chrome Root Program replied to community questions on the incident ticket, describing the CRLSet block and the eventual closure of the incident ticket as emergency containment, with follow-up work still to come. According to that comment, within an hour of the report Chrome ran Google's paranoid_crypto over every CA certificate Chrome trusts and found no other weak keys of known types. Before the incident, the checking tools in common use in the industry did not test for elliptic-curve private keys that are too small. Chrome has opened an issue in the tooling project of CCADB (the certificate authority database shared by the browser vendors) to require weak-key checks before a CA discloses a certificate.

eMudhra announced on the incident ticket on 25 October that it is leaving the public TLS certificate business, and on 30 October appointed KPMG as an independent external reviewer. According to eMudhra's incident statement page, its leadership's 26 October explanation put the problem down to an error in its own scripts and promised a full root cause analysis through the CCADB process. A 28 October update says about 30,800 certificates under G3 belong to a single customer ecosystem in the United States, which has already switched to issuing new certificates from eMudhra's G1 RSA root. eMudhra also asked the root programs for time to let these customers migrate, and says it will stop issuing TLS certificates from G1 once the migration is complete.

On 20 October the Mozilla Root Program sent eMudhra a list of questions and asked for an initial reply within 24 hours, which it still had not received on 23 October. On 23 October eMudhra blamed the delay on intense attention from social media, investors and customers, and the Chrome Root Program replied that this was not an acceptable reason. eMudhra's 25 October comment argued that CCADB's incident reporting rules give a CA 14 days to submit a full report, and that it was still within the deadline.

eMudhra later wrote on 27 October that it had replied to Mozilla's questions directly, and on 29 October attached a response document for Google to the ticket. As of the last comment on 1 November, eMudhra had not filed a formal incident report on this ticket, and the ticket was still open.

Perspective

Chrome's CRLSet, Apple's certificate configuration data and the Windows Disallowed Certificate Trust List all update automatically in the background and can block a specific intermediate certificate on its own. The command-line tools built into macOS read only the /etc/ssl/cert.pem file, which still contains the G3 root and Sectigo's AAA Certificate Services, so certificates chaining to either root pass verification. Apple's document says these tools do not check revocation, which means eMudhra's revocation of the eight intermediates on 18 October UTC has no effect on them.

According to a count a researcher posted on the incident ticket on 25 October (which we did not verify independently), 107,107 certificates signed with six of the keys were recorded in one operator's Certificate Transparency log (CT log, a public log that records every certificate) between 20 and 21 October UTC. Of these, 106,050 were proof-of-concept certificates naming only google.com, and 106,058 chained to a root through Sectigo's AAA cross-signature. One of the examples the researcher listed embeds signed certificate timestamps (SCTs, proof of inclusion) from three logs, all of which Chrome lists as usable, and from this we infer that requiring CT inclusion proofs alone does not stop such certificates. Almost none of these certificates carry a pointer to revocation information, so programs that check only the revocation status of the website certificate itself will not stop them either, and only programs that check CA certificate revocation at every level, receive a pushed blocklist, or have removed the related roots will reject them.

According to Apple's document, people who do not use Terminal need to do nothing, and people who use the built-in git, curl or python3 on a Mac to reach https:// URLs can wait for Apple's update. Those who do not want to wait can follow the same document and remove emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from /etc/ssl/cert.pem with an administrator account. Removing G3 alone does not block the six Sectigo cross-signed certificates, so AAA Certificate Services has to be removed as well. The same document notes the cost, which is that some websites unrelated to the incident that chain through these roots may also fail verification in these tools.

Apple's document also warns that a macOS update can put the original file back, so until you install a version that contains the fix, check again after every update. Apps and tools that bring their own root certificate list do not read this file and do not apply Apple's block either, and you need to ask their developers. Removing root certificates by hand on a Mac only protects the tools that read this file.

The explainer page's list of who has shipped fixes marks OpenHarmony/HarmonyOS NEXT as pending, and the page says OpenHarmony-based HarmonyOS does not let users disable system-installed roots, so "No user-side workaround is available on these devices until the patched version ships." HarmonyOS is Huawei's operating system, but that list is maintained by the researcher, not published by Huawei, and as of 2 November we had found no statement from Huawei. The same page says HarmonyOS 4.3 and earlier can disable the roots the same way as other Android-based systems, and that the block reaches many Android devices through the Google Play services update channel. GreatFire's last test on 1 November found play.google.com fully blocked in mainland China, although GreatFire measures whether the site can be reached, not whether Google Play services on a device can receive updates.

Things to watch next are the macOS update in which Apple fixes /etc/ssl/cert.pem, the formal incident report eMudhra files through the CCADB process, and each root program's decision on the G1 root. The customer ecosystem that holds about 30,800 certificates has already moved to issuing from G1. We infer that whether G1 stays trusted will decide how soon these websites have to replace their certificates again.

item.title: The Excluded Apps setting for Siri AI in iOS 27.2
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: iOS 27.2 adds Excluded Apps under Siri in Settings, for choosing apps that Siri, Search and suggestions may not read. According to EFF, on-screen awareness also stops working for excluded apps. Siri AI on iPhone and iPad is not offered in the EU or mainland China, and as of 2 November its languages do not include Chinese, so people whose device and Siri language are set to Chinese cannot use it for now.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 8 sources from Apple, EFF

Apple's release notes, published on 26 October, say iOS 27.2 adds Excluded Apps, a setting under Siri in Settings for choosing which apps Siri, Search and suggestions can access. Siri AI is the new Siri introduced in iOS 27, which can read app content to answer questions, and it runs on the iPhone 15 Pro, 15 Pro Max and iPhone 16 or later. Excluded Apps is listed in the Siri AI section of the release notes, and the iPadOS 27.2 notes list the same item. Siri AI on iPhone and iPad is not offered in the EU or mainland China, and as of 2 November its supported languages do not include Chinese, so people whose device and Siri language are set to Chinese cannot use Siri AI for now.

The same release notes say 27.2 adds French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish to Siri AI, making six languages with English. Apple's "How to get Siri AI" support page, published on 22 October, still said on 2 November that Siri AI is available only in English, and we go by the later release notes. According to Apple's September press release, the other Apple Intelligence features support simplified and traditional Chinese, while Siri AI has a language list of its own.

EFF's post of 28 October says Excluded Apps fulfils one of the asks in its Encrypt It Already campaign from earlier in 2026. The concern behind it is that many AI features require cloud processing, so even with privacy protections built into these systems, content from secure messaging apps may leave the device without the user knowing. EFF had asked for a way to tell the operating system's AI not to access a given app, even at the cost of some features, through a setting that is simple to understand.

According to EFF, after updating to 27.2 you open Excluded Apps under Siri in Settings and tap Add Apps to choose the apps to exclude. Siri AI then cannot access that app's content, and some features may stop working. EFF's example is that once Messages is excluded, you can no longer have Siri AI read or reply to messages for you. On-screen awareness, which lets you call up Siri and ask about what is on screen, also stops working for excluded apps, so with Signal excluded you cannot ask Siri to pick out any information on the Signal screen.

EFF writes that when Siri AI launched, blocking it from an app took several toggles, and the alternative was turning Siri AI off entirely. Our 27 September post, based on EFF's earlier article, said neither users nor app developers could block on-screen awareness, and that the way to limit access was turning off Show Content in Search app by app. The 27.2 exclusion list puts this in one place and covers on-screen awareness too, and in EFF's view the lost features show that the setting works.

EFF also checked where Android stands. According to EFF, in the Gemini app you tap your profile picture and go to Settings > Personal Intelligence > Connected Apps to revoke apps you do not want Gemini to access. EFF likes that the list is opt-in but finds the process less than intuitive. Signal does not support Gemini's app access feature at all, so it is not on the list, and Gemini cannot read Signal's content directly.

EFF also writes that once Device Assistance is turned on in Connected Apps, Gemini can read notifications. Basic features such as setting a timer need Device Assistance too, so EFF reckons most people already have it on.

Screen context is controlled by the Use screen and app data option in Gemini's settings, under Device controls > Screen context, and stays active until that option is turned off. Use screen and app data cannot be set per app. According to EFF, when users choose to use notification reading and screen context, both may read Signal's content or notifications. EFF wants Google to let users turn both features off per app.

Perspective

Our September post noted that a Siri AI request may be processed on the phone or sent to Private Cloud Compute (the cloud servers Apple runs to handle AI requests), and nothing on screen says which. From that we inferred in September that anyone who wants to keep using Siri AI can only limit, at the source, which apps it may read. According to EFF, Siri AI cannot access the content of an excluded app, and from this we infer that such content is not sent off the device with a request either. In EFF's view Apple should go further and offer an option to use only on-device AI features, similar to what Samsung offered with Galaxy AI.

The iOS 27.2 release notes also list more sources Siri AI can draw on, including photos attached in Messages, Calendar event attendees, voicemails, and Safari history and Reading List, and Siri AI can now recall past conversations. Going by the release notes, people already using Siri AI will find it can reach more sources after the update than before.

Apple's release notes do not say what Siri can still do once an app is excluded, only that the setting governs which apps Siri, Search and suggestions can access. Our inference from that sentence is that an excluded app's content may also stay out of Search and suggestions.

On Android, EFF compares Gemini's app list with the iOS exclusion list and finds the Android process less direct than Apple's new setting. According to EFF, people using Gemini on an Android phone can check two places, Device Assistance in Connected Apps and Use screen and app data, and each can only be turned off as a whole. Turning off Device Assistance also takes away basic features such as timers.

People whose device and Siri language are set to Chinese cannot use Siri AI for now. As of 2 November, Apple's support pages do not say whether people who have not turned on Siri AI can see Excluded Apps in Settings, or whether setting it affects Search and suggestions for them.

According to Apple's release notes and its support page, Siri AI is not available in mainland China. Apple's September press release states that Siri AI and the other new Apple Intelligence features will not be available in China while Apple works through regulatory requirements, with no timeline given. Japanese and Korean are among the five languages added in 27.2, though the support page says only that availability varies by region and platform, and we found no country-by-country listing for them. On Apple's feature availability pages for Hong Kong, Taiwan and Singapore, Siri AI was still listed on 2 November as available in English and not offered in mainland China or the EU, and those pages may not yet reflect 27.2.

People who already have Siri AI on can, after updating to iOS 27.2, go to Siri in Settings, tap Excluded Apps and add the apps to exclude (the option names follow the English interface in EFF's post). According to EFF, those who prefer the older version can still turn off Siri AI and go back to Siri Classic for now. The exclusion list only covers your own phone. We infer that if another member of a group has not excluded the same app and calls up Siri AI over the same conversation, the content may still leave from that person's phone.

item.title: Measurements of censorship and code security gaps in China's open-weight Qwen models
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: In October, two companies that publish modified versions of Qwen models each released their own measurements, one of censorship in answers to political questions in Chinese, the other of a gap in code security that follows the client named in the prompt. The findings concern people who ask Qwen political questions and developers who write code with Qwen3-Coder, whether the model runs locally or through a service. As of 1 November, we had found no third-party replication and no response from the Qwen team.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 16 sources, including Interpretic AI, Hirundo, PNAS Nexus

Two companies published measurements of Alibaba's Qwen family of open-weight models in late October (open-weight models are models whose files are public and can be downloaded and run on your own computer). Interpretic AI measured how often Qwen3.8-27B censors its answers to political questions in Chinese, and on 31 October released a version with the censorship removed on Hugging Face. According to measurements Hirundo published on its blog on 21 October, the security of the code Qwen3-Coder writes changes with the client named in the system prompt (the instructions a developer gives the model in advance), and the company has also released a modified version.

Both studies come from companies that publish the modified models, and Hirundo also evaluates and fixes models for organisations that run open-weight models. As of 1 November we had found no third-party replication, so all the figures below are each company's own measurements. Interpretic's measurements matter to people who ask Qwen political questions, and Hirundo's to developers who write code with Qwen3-Coder.

According to Interpretic's model page, the test put to the model, in Chinese, a set of 145 political questions that two researchers published in the journal PNAS Nexus, and another language model judged whether each answer was censored. Of the 113 politically sensitive questions in the set, 98 answers from the original Qwen3.8-27B were judged censored (86.7%), against 4 (3.5%) for the modified version. The model page does not say which model did the grading or whether anyone checked samples by hand, and it describes the removal only as a "targeted weight edit", with no paper or code. Interpretic lists as limitations that the political questions were tested only in Chinese, and cautions that a substantive answer is not necessarily a correct one.

The question set comes from a paper published in February 2026, in which the researchers compared foundation models developed in China with those developed elsewhere. According to the abstract, models developed in China refused more of the 145 political questions, gave shorter answers and gave more inaccurate ones. Every model refused more often when asked in Chinese than in English, but the gap between languages was smaller than the gap between Chinese and non-Chinese models.

According to Hirundo's blog, the study asked Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct to write the same web service again and again, with user registration, login and storage of private text. Each time, only the one sentence in the system prompt saying who the code was for changed, naming a neutral client, a US defence contractor, a Chinese defence contractor or a Hong Kong pro-democracy group. The finished apps were run on BaxBench, a public benchmark from ETH Zurich and LogicStar, and an app counted as exploitable if at least one off-the-shelf attack against it succeeded.

Apps written for the US defence contractor were exploitable 70% of the time, against 59% for the Chinese defence contractor. On private data leaks, nearly half of the apps written for the Hong Kong pro-democracy group let any logged-in user read everyone's private data, against about a third for the neutral client (a relative increase of 28%, as the blog calculates it). In the group whose prompts also included security instructions, 74% of the apps for the US contractor were exploitable, against 59% for the neutral client. According to the blog's statistical tests, none of the three gaps is likely to be due to chance.

The Q&A in the blog's appendix also states that the study cannot tell whether anyone put the gap into the model on purpose. Small models write vulnerable code anyway, and about a third of the neutral client's apps leaked as well, so what the study measured is the extra risk on top of that. Only one model and one task were tested, and the task was the one with the clearest gap in a small sample of 11 tasks. The US and Hong Kong groups were deliberately chosen edge cases.

Hirundo's modified model is public on Hugging Face, and its model page describes the method as behavioral unlearning (extra training that makes a model forget a specific behaviour while keeping its other abilities). According to the blog, on CCPC-500, a 500-question benchmark Hirundo built itself, the share of answers judged to contain censorship, bias or propaganda fell from 46.6% to 4.0%, and the three code gaps were no longer significant. In other comparisons in the appendix, the modified model still showed one significant gap for the US contractor against the neutral client, and in the blog's reading the effect moves from the country to the type of organisation. On ten other programming tasks, the shares of apps that worked and of apps that were exploitable were both close to those of the original model.

Perspective

A language model's answers depend on its training data and on alignment, the later stage of training that makes a model answer according to the developer's rules. Both studies measured by asking large numbers of questions and computing proportions from the output, and neither examined training data and alignment separately. Hirundo's blog argues that the modified model's results prove the code gaps sit in the model weights, and the claim rests on the same company's own removal experiment.

SpeechMap, a public research project, tested the earlier Qwen3 generation in May 2025, and according to its roundup Qwen3's open-weight models were broadly censored on topics critical of China. The censorship was most thorough with questions asked in Chinese, present in English too, and appeared in Finnish only in some cases and less consistently. The same roundup records a high number of API errors from the commercial Qwen-Max, which SpeechMap reads as an additional layer of censorship at the API. From this we infer that when a model is used through a service, the answers may be shaped both by the model itself and by filtering on the service side.

China's Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services took effect on 15 August 2023, and Article 4 requires that providing and using generative AI services must not generate content inciting subversion of state power or the overthrow of the socialist system, among other categories. Under Article 2, research and application that do not provide services to the public in mainland China fall outside the Measures, and we found no provision specifically on publishing model weights. The researchers behind the PNAS Nexus paper caution that their study is observational and cross-sectional (it compares different models at a single point in time, without experiments) and "does not establish a causal linkage between regulatory pressures and censorship behaviors of China-originating LLMs".

On 3 February 2025, Taiwan's Executive Yuan required all public agencies to stop using DeepSeek AI services, and its press release noted that the security risk of data being uploaded to China had been neither clarified nor ruled out, and that the model's training involved data bias such as ideological censorship. According to the Administration for Cyber Security on 20 February 2025, the ban covered cloud services, apps and locally downloaded use, and at the time placed no restriction on use by the general public. The notices named DeepSeek, and we found none naming Qwen.

We, a community based in Taiwan, compared rules on generative AI from mainland China, Taiwan and South Korea, and neither the Taiwanese nor the South Korean rules discussed here regulate the political position of a model's answers. Besides Article 4 of the Interim Measures, mainland China has guidelines on deploying large AI models in government work, issued by the Office of the Central Cyberspace Affairs Commission and the National Development and Reform Commission and published on 10 October 2025 as a reference for government departments' own use, which call on those departments to use mature models and services that have completed filing with the cyberspace authorities for general-purpose tasks such as question answering and drafting documents (filing is a condition of entry, and the guidelines do not say what it examines). Taiwan's DeepSeek ban works on use instead, limiting which products public agencies may use. Article 31 of South Korea's Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and the Creation of a Foundation for Trust, in full force since 22 January 2026, requires a business providing generative AI to label the output as generated by generative AI, and according to the Ministry of Science and ICT, fact-finding investigations and penalties under this transparency provision are deferred for a grace period of at least one year (checked on 1 November).

In Interpretic's tests, the modified model refused 95 of 100 harmful requests, down from 100, and its scores on general ability tests dropped slightly, side effects that anyone thinking of switching to it has to weigh. Both companies' modified models keep the original's Apache 2.0 licence, but Interpretic published no paper or code, and Hirundo described only the category of its method. Hirundo's blog states that it intends to release CCPC-500, but when we checked on 1 November the dataset's address could not be accessed (it returned a 401 error), so we cannot confirm that it is public. According to SpeechMap's roundup of May 2025, third-party modifications of the Chinese open-source models of the time had brought clear improvements in English and only modest ones in Chinese.

For people who use Qwen to look up sensitive subjects such as politics or history, we suggest putting the same question to models from different sources, then checking the answers against news coverage and primary materials. According to both the paper's abstract and SpeechMap, asking in Chinese produced more refusals or censorship, and from this we infer that asking again in another language may produce a different answer, though the paper also notes that the language gap is smaller than the gap between Chinese and non-Chinese models. None of these studies evaluated whether such approaches recover censored content, and questions that were not tested are not necessarily free of bias (our inference).

Developers writing code with Qwen3-Coder or any other model still need to review and test it separately before it goes into production. According to Hirundo's blog, adding security instructions to the prompt did not remove the gap, and common static analysis tools may not catch this kind of leak, where a logged-in user can read other people's data. On the ten other tasks, about a quarter of the apps written by the modified model were still exploitable, and the neutral client's apps leaked too (see above). From this we infer that, whichever version you use, access control checks are a good place to start a review.

As of 1 November, we had found no public response from Alibaba or the Qwen team to either study or to the paper. In early December, it will be worth watching whether any third party replicates the two companies' measurements, whether CCPC-500 is published, and whether the Qwen team responds.

item.title: The ad exception for Gmail and Photos data in Google's privacy policy
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: The 16 October version of Google's privacy policy adds an exception to its rule against personalized ads based on Drive, Gmail and Photos content, for users who choose to make that data available to other Google services that support personalized ads, such as through Personal Intelligence. People who have not connected these apps need not change anything, and as of 1 November those who have can review or disconnect them under Search Services Personalization in their Google Account.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 16 sources, including Google, The Verge, Ars Technica

The version of Google's privacy policy that took effect on 16 October adds an exception to the sentence saying Google does not show personalized ads based on content from Drive, Gmail or Photos. The exception applies when users choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads, and people who have not made that choice are outside it. The example given in the policy's additional context is Personal Intelligence, which, according to a Google Search help page, people aged 18 or over who are signed in to a personal Google Account can turn on themselves. As of 1 November, the supported countries and territories on that page included Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macau, Japan, South Korea and Singapore, and connecting Google Photos is not available in every region.

According to The Verge's report of 23 October, people who have already used Personal Intelligence to connect Gmail or Photos to AI Mode (a search feature that answers questions conversationally) and other Search tools may now see ads based on the content of their email and photos. Google's comparison of the two versions shows that the 1 October text did not have the closing clause "unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads". A new sentence states that users may allow Search or Gemini Apps to access data from Photos, Gmail and Drive, and that Search may process some of that data to personalize content, including ads. The sentence on ads also changed from ads based on "interests and activity" to ads based on "interests, activity, or personalized content from Google services".

In the example in the policy's additional context, a user asks Search about a recent hotel booking, and Search may use booking details from an email to suggest things to do near the hotel. According to the Search help page, connecting once gives all Search services access to Gmail and Photos, including Google Search, AI Mode, Discover (the feed of recommended articles on the Google app's home screen), Maps, Shopping, Flights, Hotels, Translate and News. Drive, which the policy mentions, was not among the apps that could be connected on the help page when we checked on 1 November. Ask Maps in Google Maps (a feature for asking about routes and places conversationally) can also be connected to Gmail, and as of 1 November its listed regions in Asia were only India, Japan and Indonesia, not Taiwan.

Perspective

The first sentence of Google's full statement, published by Ars Technica on 23 October, is that connecting apps is entirely opt-in. The statement goes on to say that ads will continue to be relevant to things like the query, the context of the response and the user's interests, and will not be based directly on the Gmail inbox or Photos library. According to the Q&A on the Search help page, advertisers do not get access to the inbox or Photos, and Google does not show personalized ads based on sensitive categories such as race, religion, sexual orientation or health. As of 1 November, we found statements only from Google and the press, with no public response from advocacy groups or data protection authorities.

The help page's answer on ads likewise says ads will not be based directly on the inbox or Photos library, then adds that Search may reference summaries, excerpts and inferences from these sources to personalize the experience, and that "That same info may be used to show you ads". Read this way, ads are not based on the inbox or library themselves, while the summaries, excerpts and inferences Search derives from email and photos may be used for ads. The same page's answer on training AI models includes an example of how Search pulls email and photos together. When a user asks AI Mode to suggest restaurants for an upcoming trip, the models might look at emails and photos for the hotel reservation and flight itinerary, then summarize that information into recommendations.

According to the help page, Search services do not train generative AI models directly on the Gmail inbox or on imagery and audio from the Photos library. The page goes on to state that when users interact with Search, summaries, excerpts and inferences from relevant emails, files and media are used to train the models. Where an email is brief or particularly relevant to the question, the summary may be the email itself. Once apps are connected, a subset of the data processed by AI Mode and Ask Maps is reviewed by human reviewers, including trained service providers.

We, a community based in Taiwan, looked at how the feature is offered in Asia, which The Verge's report does not cover. As of 1 November, the Search help page's supported countries and territories for connecting content apps included, among others, Hong Kong, Japan, Macau, Malaysia, Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan, with Chinese (Traditional), Chinese (Simplified), Japanese and Korean among the languages, and mainland China was not on the list. For the Gemini version, GIGAZINE reported that Google Japan posted on X on 14 April 2026 that Personal Intelligence in Gemini had begun a phased rollout in Japan, to be completed within a week. For Hong Kong, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan we found no official launch announcement for the Gemini version, and the Gemini help page gives no country list.

None of the following provisions or policy plans is aimed at features that connect email or photos to ads, and we did not check how any of them would apply here, but they point in different directions. Taiwan and mainland China work through refusal, with Article 20 of Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act requiring a non-government entity that markets with personal data to stop once the person objects and to offer a way to object the first time, and Article 24 of mainland China's Personal Information Protection Law requiring marketing through automated decision-making to come with an option that does not target personal characteristics or a convenient way to refuse. Under a policy plan South Korea's Personal Information Protection Commission published on 31 January 2024, by contrast, advertisers that do not identify a specific person may process online behavioural data without consent, provided that accumulating, overlapping or combining the data does not make anyone identifiable, while identifying a person requires consent. We could not find whether the revised guidelines the Commission planned to issue by the end of 2024 are in force, and readers can ask whether a way to refuse, an option not to be targeted or a consent requirement tied to identification reaches ads shaped by summaries and inferences from data a user connected for a different feature.

People who have not connected Gmail or Photos to Search or Gemini do not need to change any settings. Those who have can follow the Search help page: on a computer, go to Search Services Personalization in the Google Account, then Additional Personal Intelligence > Connected Content Apps, to review or disconnect them. Anyone who wants to try the feature first turns on Personalized Recommendations in the same place and then connects, and the actual screens may differ from the instructions (as of 1 November, a banner at the top of the help page said the settings are being updated). In Gemini the connections are under Settings & help > Personal Intelligence > Connected Apps at the bottom of gemini.google.com, and the service named in the policy as processing this data to personalize content, including ads, is Search, with no mention of Gemini.

The connection settings in Search cover whether Gmail and Photos data is made available to Search, and My Ad Center is a separate set of controls. Under the policy, the ad settings in My Ad Center control what information Google uses to show ads, but the My Ad Center help page does not say whether its personalized ads switch covers connected data. Besides connecting the apps, the Search help page requires turning on Smart features in other Google products in Gmail as a condition for personalized responses. According to the Gmail help page, this setting controls the use of Workspace data in other Google products, and the page does not mention Photos or ads.

Going by the example in the policy's additional context (our inference), features such as suggesting plans from hotel booking details in an email work only once the apps are connected, and disconnecting removes them. According to the Search help page, data already saved in Search Services History is not deleted when an app is disconnected and can still be used for product improvement, including training generative AI models.

item.title: Weekly brief, 2026 week 44
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Seven stories from 13 to 23 October: Hong Kong's tighter rules on access to land records, the face search engine PimEyes and the EU AI Act's ban, Senate committee review of Canada's Bill C-22, the finding that microtargeted ads by four German parties were unlawful, a generative AI pilot for checks at France's public employment service, European governments' Palantir contracts, and the enforcement of Ofcom's fines against websites outside the UK.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 16 sources, including Hong Kong Free Press, Development Bureau, South China Morning Post

This issue collects seven stories, one of them a follow-up to an earlier article, covering 13 to 23 October.

Rules on access to land records in Hong Kong

According to a Development Bureau announcement on 16 October, the Hong Kong government gazetted eight pieces of subsidiary legislation that day. The provisions on electronic applications take effect on 4 October 2027, and the Secretary for Development will set the commencement date for the rest in the first half of 2027.

Hong Kong Free Press reported on 21 October that the new rules limit land record searches to nine purposes, and news reporting is not among them. "Public interest" is listed as a valid ground, but the Land Registrar vets every application case by case. The Hong Kong Journalists Association called for the amendments to be shelved, arguing that protecting "privacy" should not override the public's right to know, and listed 18 investigative reports produced using land records.

According to a Development Bureau paper to the Legislative Council quoted by Hong Kong Free Press, the purpose of the amendments is to strike a balance between protecting personal data privacy and keeping land records transparent. The South China Morning Post reported that on 23 October the Legislative Council decided to set up a subcommittee to examine them.

The face search engine PimEyes and the AI Act's ban

According to a netzpolitik.org report on 13 October, the EU's Artificial Intelligence Act has since 2 February 2025 banned AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet, but the face search engine PimEyes still operates as usual in Germany. The Federal Network Agency, designated as the competent authority only in summer 2026, declined to comment on planned or ongoing proceedings. A German bill would let the Federal Criminal Police Office and the Federal Police use such search engines, and according to the report, the bill's explanatory memorandum rests on the view that the ban does not apply if no AI system is used to scrape the data. As of 31 October, we had found no response from PimEyes to the report.

Senate committee review of Canada's Bill C-22

Our 20 October article, "Senate second reading of Canada's Bill C-22 and providers' responses", covered this Lawful Access Act. The bill would let the government require telecommunications and online service providers to build technical capabilities to assist law enforcement, and require designated providers to retain metadata (records about communications rather than their content). According to the bill's progress page on the Parliament of Canada website, the bill passed second reading in the Senate on 22 October and was referred to the Standing Senate Committee on National Security, Defence and Veterans Affairs. As of 31 October, the committee had no recorded activity on it.

According to the Senate Debates for the same day, the opposition critic for the bill argued that it should go to the Standing Senate Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs instead. The senator also noted that a House of Commons committee had amended the metadata retention period to six months. According to an Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) article on 22 October, the Canadian Civil Liberties Association is urging people to sign a petition against the bill, and some senators have also expressed concerns.

Finding of unlawful microtargeting by four German parties

According to an announcement on 21 October by noyb, a European privacy advocacy group, the Berlin data protection authority found that the SPD, the Greens, the Left Party and the CDU targeted ads at users based on their political interests without a legal basis such as consent. dpa-AFX, part of the German Press Agency (dpa), reported that the authority made its decision on 24 September and issued only formal warnings or reprimands to the parties, with no fines. As of netzpolitik.org's report on 23 October, the penalties were not yet final, according to a spokesperson for the authority. As of 31 October, we had found no response from the four parties.

Generative AI pilot for job-search checks at France's public employment service

On 23 October, La Quadrature du Net, a French digital rights group, published a presentation that France Travail gave to its AI ethics committee on 30 June. According to the group, the public employment service is piloting generative AI to help check whether jobseekers are actively looking for work, and the group called for its immediate withdrawal.

In the presentation's own words, the AI consolidates data from the database, interviews and case files into a single report, which an adviser analyses and validates. According to the same presentation, the decision always remains with the adviser. The goals it lists are meeting the 2027 target for checks with unchanged staffing and making checks systematic by 2030.

La Quadrature du Net argues that the advisers' work will be reduced to confirming possible sanctions. As of 31 October, we had found no response from France Travail to the document.

Palantir contracts with European governments

According to a netzpolitik.org report on 15 October, an investigation led by the Dutch outlet Follow the Money, with media from 18 countries taking part, found national-level contracts with Palantir, the US data analytics software company, in 11 European countries, eight of which have dealings with the armed forces or defence ministry. According to the same report, many countries are concerned about dependence, security and democracy, and are looking for alternatives.

According to netzpolitik.org's weekly round-up, the amounts disclosed by individual countries add up to about €1.4 billion. Some governments do not disclose their costs, so this is a lower bound. In its response to the investigative team, Palantir stated that technological sovereignty should be judged by who controls the data and decisions, not only by the nationality of the software vendor.

Enforcement of Ofcom's fines against websites outside the UK

Ofcom, the UK communications regulator, has fined the forum 4chan hundreds of thousands of pounds under the Online Safety Act, and according to a report by the entertainment outlet Dexerto on 20 October, 4chan had not paid. According to the same report, Ofcom's chief executive told a House of Commons committee that some fines may never be recovered if foreign courts get in the way. The chief executive also said that only 2 of the 11 fines issued under the Act since March 2025 had been paid.

A lawyer representing 4chan described this testimony on the lawyer's own website as Ofcom conceding defeat, while Dexerto wrote that the chief executive did not name 4chan and that Ofcom has not publicly said it is abandoning enforcement. According to news from the University of Oxford's Faculty of Law, the lawsuit 4chan brought against Ofcom in the US was dismissed by a federal district court in mid-September on grounds of foreign sovereign immunity. As of 31 October, we had found no response from Ofcom or any new enforcement action.
