item.title: Dispute over the removal of the Bluetooth mesh messaging app Bitchat in India
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Bitchat, an open-source messaging app that sends messages over a Bluetooth mesh network without the internet, was removed from the App Store in India on 3 October at the request of India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. As of 31 October, neither the order nor its reasons had been published, and on 11 November the Kerala High Court will hear a public interest petition seeking to suspend the block. Readers outside India are not affected by this removal.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 17 sources, including TechCrunch, SFLC.in, Internet Freedom Foundation

Bitchat, an open-source messaging app that sends messages over a Bluetooth mesh network (phones relay messages to one another without going through the internet), was removed from the App Store in India on 3 October. According to the Apple notice the developer made public, the removal followed a demand from India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, and no illegal content was identified in it. When TechCrunch checked that day, Bitchat could not be found on Google Play in India either, and Apple, Google and MeitY did not respond to requests for comment. The removal applies only in India, and as of 31 October the App Store lookup interface still returned Bitchat for Taiwan and Hong Kong, though not for mainland China, where it was removed separately in February (see Perspective).

Under Section 69A, the central government may, in the interest of sovereignty, defence, state security, public order and similar grounds, direct intermediaries by an order with reasons recorded in writing to block public access to information. Under the 2009 Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, the designated officer is to make all reasonable efforts to notify the person or intermediary hosting the information to appear before a committee chaired by the designated officer, with representatives of the law, home affairs and other ministries. In an emergency, the ministry's secretary may issue directions without a hearing, and the designated officer must bring the request before the committee within 48 hours. Under the same rules, all blocking requests and actions taken must be kept confidential.

As of 31 October, we, a community based in Taiwan, had found no public explanation from the government for the October removal, and two Indian digital rights groups, SFLC.in and the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF), both wrote in statements in early October that the order and its reasons could not be found. Bitchat's developer has only posted Apple's notice on X, and we found no formal response or legal action. In its notice, Apple asks the developer to contact MeitY directly.

The government reasons we did find come from a different notice in July. On 23 July, the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre of the Ministry of Home Affairs, relying on a different provision, asked GitHub to remove Bitchat's code repositories, on the grounds that apps of this kind need no registration or phone number verification and that their architecture impedes lawful interception and law enforcement investigations. According to the same notice, such tools could be used to coordinate unlawful activity during internet shutdowns or public order incidents. According to IFF and the Indian tech policy outlet MediaNama, the July notices were reportedly withdrawn or not enforced after they became public.

Perspective

Bitchat lets nearby phones relay messages directly, up to 7 hops, with no account or phone number. When a connection is available, messages can also travel through relays on Nostr (an open, decentralised messaging protocol). According to the developer's documentation, private messages are encrypted with the Noise protocol (a framework for setting up encrypted sessions). Live sessions have forward secrecy (a key leaked later cannot decrypt earlier messages), while messages stored for offline delivery do not.

According to the developer's privacy assessment, public channel content is visible to everyone taking part. Device identifiers do not rotate, so people nearby can recognise the same device across time and places, and can tell that someone is using the app.

Bitchat is maintained by volunteers, and the iOS version is released into the public domain (anyone may freely use and modify the code). Soon after its launch in July 2025, a researcher pointed out that its identity verification was open to a man-in-the-middle attack (a third party impersonating one side of a conversation), and the security firm Trail of Bits wrote in a commentary that it should not be relied on for sensitive messages at the time. The developer then moved to Noise encryption, and according to a fix merged in June 2026, one audit found ten critical or high-risk issues. The auditor is not named in the fix, and as of 31 October we had found no complete audit report from an independent organisation.

According to SFLC.in's statement, the block appears to have no end date, and using Section 69A to block an entire messaging app is disproportionate. IFF's position is that the block is unconstitutional: Section 69A permits blocking unlawful information, and a messaging tool that works during internet shutdowns falls outside that. In the Telegram case in June, the Delhi High Court held that Section 69A can be used to block an entire app, and according to the committee opinion quoted in that judgment, that block was temporary and limited in duration.

SFLC.in notes in its statement that the removal came right after an internet shutdown on 2 October, and infers that the app may have been targeted because it allows communication during shutdowns. IFF's view is that the government objects to what the app can do, not to the content it carries. The government's reasoning in the July notice is that the architecture of such apps impedes lawful interception, and that because they keep working during shutdowns and network restrictions, they could be used to get around those restrictions.

Blocking requests are to be kept confidential under the 2009 rules, yet Apple passed the notice on to the developer. IFF is asking the government to publish the order and its reasons, and Apple to disclose the demand in its transparency report, and says it will seek a copy of the order under the Right to Information Act (the law that lets people request information from public authorities). On 14 October, the Kerala High Court heard a public interest litigation (a case brought in the public interest) and, without yet deciding whether it is maintainable, directed all respondents to file affidavits first, with the next hearing on 11 November. The respondents include government ministries and the Indian subsidiaries of Apple and Google.

According to IFF's statement, the removal does not delete the app from phones where it is already installed, but new users cannot download it and existing users stop receiving security updates. Anyone considering Bitchat can start with the white paper and privacy assessment the developer publishes on GitHub. According to these documents, public channel content is visible to everyone taking part, people nearby can detect a device running the app, and security fixes ship only in the latest version.

The iOS version requires iOS 16 or later and the Android version requires Android 8.0 or later, and both offer Traditional and Simplified Chinese interfaces. For people who care about being recognised by those nearby, this risk remains after they start using the app, and the developer lists rotating identifiers as future work.

In February 2026, the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) also asked Apple to remove Bitchat from the App Store in mainland China. According to the notice the developer made public in April, summarised by the Japanese tech outlet GIGAZINE, Apple named the provision relied on: Article 3 of the Provisions on the Security Assessment of Internet-based Information Services with Attribute of Public Opinions or Capable of Social Mobilization. As of 31 October, the App Store lookup interface returned no result for Bitchat in mainland China.

Under Article 3, providers of services with public opinion attributes or social mobilisation capability must carry out their own security assessments when, for example, they launch such a service, add such features or see users grow significantly, and removal is not mentioned in the article itself. Under the same provisions, a provider that has not done an assessment is first notified to do one, and one that refuses faces a public risk warning and inspection, and any violations found are to be dealt with according to law. The provisions themselves do not mention an appeal or a court, and we did not check general administrative review or judicial review. We found no published order and no end date.

According to media reports, Taiwan's Ministry of the Interior publicly announced action against Xiaohongshu (RedNote) in December 2025, requiring network access providers under the Fraud Crime Hazard Prevention Act to stop resolving its domains (so that addresses no longer lead to its servers) and restrict access, for a provisional period of one year. Unlike India's case, where neither the order nor its reasons are public, the government announced this action and cited the law. It was directed at network access providers, and app stores are not mentioned in the reports. We checked only that act and the Copyright Act, which often comes up in discussions of website blocking and in its current form contains no provision for ordering blocks, and found no provision empowering the government to order an app store to remove a particular app.

In Hong Kong, we also found no provision that specifically empowers the government to order an app store to remove a particular app. Under Schedule 4 of the Implementation Rules for Article 43 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Safeguarding National Security in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (as published in 2020; we have not checked later amendments), a designated officer authorised by the Commissioner of Police with the approval of the Secretary for Security may require a platform service provider to take a disabling action on an electronic message likely to constitute an offence endangering national security, without first going to a court. Schedule 4 is about electronic messages on electronic platforms, app stores are not mentioned in it, and we have not checked whether its "platform service provider" includes them.

Under Schedule 4, requirements must be in writing. A service provider charged with failing to comply has a defence if compliance could not reasonably be expected because the necessary technology was not reasonably available, or because of a risk of substantial loss to, or substantial prejudice to the rights of, a third party. Schedule 4 itself has no provision on giving reasons or a route of appeal, and we did not check general judicial review.

For both the Indian and the mainland Chinese removals, we found no published order and no end date, and Apple named only the legal basis in its notices. India's rules require the designated officer to make all reasonable efforts to notify the host or intermediary to appear before a committee, though in an emergency directions can be issued without a hearing, and a public interest petition against this removal has been filed, with the court yet to decide whether it is maintainable. In mainland China, Article 12 of the assessment provisions does provide for prior notice, but the notice asks the provider to carry out an assessment, rather than giving the developer a chance to be heard before removal. Taiwan's action against Xiaohongshu was announced publicly with the law and a one-year term, but it targeted network access rather than an app store.

When comparing approaches, it helps to ask whether a removal order is published, whether it gives reasons and an end date, and whether developers and users have a chance to be heard before removal or to seek a remedy afterwards. The intended effect of the policy belongs in the comparison too. Removal does not delete installed copies of the app, and we could find no public assessment of whether the block achieves the law enforcement aims the government has stated.

item.title: Norway's fine on Xandr over Grindr user data in real-time bidding
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: On 12 October, Norway's data protection authority announced a fine of NOK 92 million (about €8.5 million) on Xandr, an advertising technology company owned by Microsoft, for processing data on Grindr users in Norway through real-time bidding from 2018 to 2020 without a legal basis. A Microsoft spokesperson told the press the conduct predates the acquisition and the company is reviewing the decision. Users can delete the advertising ID or refuse tracking in phone settings, and the official help pages do not say whether those settings cover the other data named in the decision.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 21 sources, including Datatilsynet, noyb, netzpolitik.org

The Norwegian Data Protection Authority (Datatilsynet) announced on 12 October a fine of NOK 92 million (about €8.5 million according to the decision) on Xandr, an advertising technology company owned by Microsoft, the highest fine the authority had issued at the time of the announcement. According to the decision of 2 October, Xandr had no legal basis when it processed data on Grindr users in Norway through real-time bidding from July 2018 to April 2020, and the data included at least the fact that a person used Grindr, the advertising ID (an identifier the phone's operating system assigns to each device for advertising) and the IP address. The fine covers only users in Norway, and the decision contains no assessment of current practice. According to an explainer the authority published on 16 October, every time someone opens an app with ads, this kind of auction may be triggered.

Real-time bidding (RTB) is the mechanism by which an app or website with ad space sends user data to advertising platforms so that advertisers can bid for it within a fraction of a second. According to the decision, when a user opened Grindr, the ad request went to Xandr either directly or through MoPub, an ad mediation service. Xandr ran platforms on both the seller and buyer sides at the time, and according to the authority's press release the data could be passed on to thousands of companies.

In its decision, the authority held that using Grindr is itself information that indicates sexual orientation, which makes it special category personal data under the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR, which also applies in the European Economic Area that Norway belongs to). Processing such data is prohibited in principle, and explicit consent is one of the exceptions. According to the authority's press release, Xandr's defence was that it thought Grindr had obtained users' consent. The authority concluded that the consent Grindr collected was invalid, and that Xandr, as a joint controller (one of the companies jointly deciding how data is processed), had to verify for itself that consent was valid and could not pass the responsibility on to others.

The case grew out of complaints the Norwegian Consumer Council and noyb, a European privacy advocacy group, filed in 2020 against Grindr and several adtech companies. Grindr itself was fined NOK 65 million in December 2021, a fine upheld in turn by the Privacy Appeals Board, the Oslo District Court and the Court of Appeal. According to the authority's annual report for 2025, the Court of Appeal's judgment of October 2025 was not appealed further and is final.

Perspective

A Microsoft spokesperson told netzpolitik.org, a German digital policy outlet, that the investigation and decision concern conduct before Microsoft acquired Xandr, and that the interpretation of legal standards and practice has developed since. The spokesperson added that the company is reviewing the decision and evaluating its options.

According to the decision, Xandr argued that when the investigation began, neither it nor any company in the same position could have foreseen the standards and conclusions the authority applied. The authority took this to mean industry practice, and citing the Court of Appeal, held that industry practice cannot count as a mitigating factor.

The fine was calculated on Xandr's own annual turnover. Relying on case law of the Court of Justice of the EU, the authority found that because Xandr was not part of Microsoft during the period of the infringement, using Microsoft's turnover would be neither appropriate nor necessary.

Xandr objected to basing the fine on revenue for the 2025 fiscal year, because the authority took more than a year after its advance notification (the notice before a decision) to issue the decision. The authority still used that year's revenue, but counted the long handling time as a mitigating factor and reduced the fine. Xandr also argued that the delay had harmed its ability to defend itself, which the authority did not accept.

The deadline to appeal is three weeks from receipt of the decision, and the date of receipt has not been made public. As of 31 October, the authority's English news page had no follow-up announcement.

On 12 October, noyb linked the fine to the EU's Digital Omnibus (a proposal the European Commission put forward in November 2025 to simplify digital rules), arguing that industry lobbying aims to take identifiers used for online tracking out of the GDPR. The European consumer organisation BEUC, for its part, is concerned that loosening the definition of personal data would leave the kind of consent practice found unlawful in this case without constraint.

According to the Council of the EU's press release of 21 October, the position agreed by member states keeps the existing definition of personal data and adds new provisions on pseudonymisation (replacing fields that directly identify a person with codes).

The same press release states that the new provisions aim to make it clearer to organisations how to comply. In noyb's reading of 23 October, the new pseudonymisation provisions would drastically narrow what counts as personal data.

On Android, the advertising ID can be deleted under Settings > Privacy > Ads, and on an iPhone, Settings > Privacy & Security > Tracking lets you turn off "Allow Apps to Request to Track", or turn tracking off app by app. Under Apple's rules for apps, once a user asks an app not to track, the app may not track the user with other information that identifies the user or the device either. According to Google's help page, apps may have their own settings using other types of identifiers. Neither company's page says whether the IP address and which app is in use are still sent with ad requests, so we cannot confirm whether these settings cover the other data named in the decision.

The decision contains no information about users or current practice in Asia. We, a community based in Taiwan, compared Taiwan, Japan and mainland China on two points from the case: whether using an app counts as sensitive data, and whether each company along the ad chain has to deal with consent itself. We did not check how regulators or courts in these places interpret the use of a particular app.

Article 6 of Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act lists data on sex life, together with medical records, genetic data and criminal records, as data that in principle may not be collected, processed or used, with written consent as one of the exceptions, subject to limits: such consent does not count where the use goes beyond what the specific purpose requires or is against the person's will. The article does not mention sexual orientation. We did not check whether every company along an ad chain has to deal with consent itself under the Act, which has no provision specifically on advertising identifiers or real-time bidding.

Under Article 20 of Japan's Act on the Protection of Personal Information, acquiring "special care-required personal information" requires the person's prior consent outside the listed exceptions. The categories in the Act and its Cabinet Order include race, creed, social status, medical history and criminal record, and neither they nor the general guidelines of the Personal Information Protection Commission list sexual orientation.

The Commission's guidelines give browsing histories collected through cookies and other device identifiers, and records of the services a person uses, as examples of "personally referable information". Under Article 31, when the recipient is expected to acquire such information as personal data identifying the person, the company providing it has to confirm beforehand that the person's consent has been obtained. According to section 3-7-2-2 of the guidelines, the consent is to be obtained by the recipient, which deals with the person and uses the information, though the provider may obtain it on the recipient's behalf, provided the person's rights are equally protected.

In Norway the company receiving the data was held responsible for checking the consent collected upstream, while for personally referable information under Article 31 the check sits with the company providing it (our comparison). A company acquiring special care-required personal information has to obtain the person's prior consent itself under Article 20(2). Article 30(1) separately requires a company receiving personal data from a third party to confirm the provider's name and address and how the provider acquired the data, unless an exception in Article 27(1) or (5) applies.

Article 28 of mainland China's Personal Information Protection Law lists biometrics, religious belief, specific identity, medical health, financial accounts, whereabouts and similar information as sensitive personal information, without mentioning sexual orientation, and under Article 29 handling sensitive personal information requires the person's separate consent. A January 2026 Q&A by the Cyberspace Administration of China, citing the national standard GB/T 45574-2025, lists common categories of sensitive personal information without sexual orientation, and we did not read the standard itself.

The Norwegian conclusion concerned Xandr's responsibility as a joint controller, which corresponds to Article 20 of the Chinese law (our comparison). Handlers that jointly decide the purpose and method of processing must agree on their respective rights and duties, and under Article 20(2) they are jointly and severally liable for harm to rights and interests in personal information. Providing personal information to another handler is a different relationship covered by Article 23, under which the provider itself has to tell the person who the recipient is, its purpose and the types of information and obtain separate consent, while the recipient has to stay within that purpose, method and scope or obtain consent again. Unlike Japan's Article 31, where the provider confirms that consent has been obtained, Article 23 has the provider obtain the consent (our comparison), and we did not check whether passing data along an ad chain counts as joint processing or as provision under Chinese law.

Comparing approaches across places, readers can ask whether using an app is treated as sensitive data, and whether every company along the ad chain that receives the data has to verify consent itself. Another question is how regulators assess past practice when a company argues that the interpretation of legal standards has since developed. If other places follow the Digital Omnibus in adjusting the definition of personal data, whether identifiers used for tracking remain covered is also worth comparing. The intended effect of the policy matters too: this case went from complaint in 2020 to decision in 2026, and the question is whether the fine can change what companies do now.

item.title: Content takedown disputes in Indonesia and a civil society coalition weighing legal action
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: In October, the Indonesian digital rights group SAFEnet reviewed two years of digital controls under the current government and recorded at least 73 pieces of content taken down between April and September 2026, most of them critical of the government. SAFEnet and other groups are also gathering potential plaintiffs to assess legal action against the Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs. The ministry denies asking platforms to restrict content about forest fires, and in September the Constitutional Court ruled that the government must give notice with reasons before cutting off access. Readers outside Indonesia are not directly affected.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 18 sources, including SAFEnet, Pasal.id, Bisnis.com

On 21 October, the Indonesian digital rights group SAFEnet published a report on two years of digital controls under the current president and vice president, arguing that digital space is increasingly becoming a site of repression, surveillance and censorship. By SAFEnet's count, 5,549 digital rights violations were recorded from 2025 to mid-2026, a figure we could not check against any independent source. On 23 October, a legal team formed by SAFEnet with a journalists' association, legal aid groups and others opened a desk to hear from people whose content has been restricted. The restrictions apply inside Indonesia, and readers elsewhere are not directly affected.

According to SAFEnet's report, it and the media monitoring group Remotivi recorded at least 73 pieces of content taken down between April and September 2026, most of them criticising the president, the free nutritious meals programme or disaster response. A separate SAFEnet statement of 5 October gives the period as April to August, and says 90.4% were moderated or removed at the request of the Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs (Komdigi). According to the same statement, the notices platforms sent on the ministry's request never stated which law had been broken. We found no public response from Komdigi to the figures of 73 items and 90.4%.

The National Commission on Human Rights (Komnas HAM) questioned Komdigi after receiving complaints of "internet restrictions" and "social media restrictions" during protests. On 13 October a commissioner relayed Komdigi's account that it removed 486 pieces of suspected illegal content, based on its online patrols, on 27 August, the day of large-scale protests. Komdigi also denied that it restricted the internet. The commission is still examining the legal basis for those removals.

Komdigi's own figures show about 4.2 million pieces of illegal content removed between October 2024 and April 2026, mostly online gambling and pornography. These are the ministry's own numbers, which we also could not check independently. The 486, the 4.2 million and SAFEnet's 73 are three different counts and cannot be added together or compared.

In mid-October, public figures said their posts about forest fires were reaching fewer people. Komdigi's deputy minister and then the minister denied that the ministry had asked platforms to remove or restrict information about the fires. In a video statement on 21 October, the minister also said the ministry is pushing for accountability and transparency in platform algorithms, and asked users to appeal to the platform first and then report to the ministry.

The legal team has not said in its press release what it would sue over or in which court. According to the release, filling in the form does not make someone a plaintiff, and that the choice of plaintiffs depends on evidence, harm and standing (whether a person is entitled to bring the case). The team also asks people to include screenshots of moderation notices from the platform, links to the content, and their correspondence with the platform.

Perspective

Ministerial Decree 127/2026, signed by Komdigi in March, classifies disinformation and hate speech as content that causes public unrest, and requires platforms to carry out an access cut-off order from the minister within four hours of receiving it. We could not find the decree itself, so its content here follows Kontan's quotations. According to the director for digital space control interviewed by Kontan, reported content is first reviewed jointly with the relevant ministries and agencies. Objections to the government are filed by the platform through SAMAN (the system the ministry uses to send orders to platforms and track compliance), and the ministry separately encourages platforms to offer users a way to object.

The ministry's reasons are set out in the considerations of the decree: disinformation and hate speech can cause public unrest, panic and conflict between groups. Before the decree was issued, the director general of digital space supervision also said in September 2025, when discussing SAMAN, that takedowns are not meant to silence criticism. In April, the Alliance of Independent Journalists (AJI) called for the decree to be revoked, arguing that terms like "causing public unrest" are too vague.

According to a commentary published by the University of Melbourne's Indonesia research outlet, a March Instagram post by the independent outlet Magdalene, which introduced an investigative report on an acid attack, was restricted inside Indonesia under this decree and the restriction was lifted a few days later. The commentary quotes the director general as saying the post's narrative and title could mislead the public and trigger distrust of state institutions, and that Magdalene is not on the Press Council's list of verified outlets. A Press Council member said Magdalene is a legitimate news organisation and that Press Council verification is not a legal requirement.

In its ruling of 29 September (311/PUU-XXIV/2026), the Constitutional Court declared the provision of the Electronic Information and Transactions Law that authorises the government to cut off access conditionally unconstitutional: the government must first issue a digital or written notice with reasons before it cuts off access or orders a platform to do so. The court did not accept the petitioners' argument that prior court approval should be required. As of 29 October, we had not obtained any public statement from Komdigi on the ruling, and found nothing on whether it has changed how it gives notice. SAFEnet calls the ruling a first step towards reform, and argues that because the ministry is both regulator and enforcer, notice alone does not guarantee that restrictions are proportionate.

OONI (Open Observatory of Network Interference, censorship measurements run by volunteers in many countries) and Cloudflare Radar (traffic monitoring) measure whether websites can be reached and overall traffic, so the removal of a single post or a drop in reach does not show up in their data. OONI's website connectivity measurements show no spike in anomalies on 27 August, and Radar has no outage annotation for Indonesia from late August to early September (checked on 29 October). OONI's coverage depends on where volunteers are and is uneven across telecom operators, so regional or operator-level interference cannot be ruled out.

For people whose content has been restricted or removed by a platform in Indonesia, the minister's suggested route is to appeal to the platform first and then report to the ministry. Keeping screenshots of notices and links to the content gives a basis for any later appeal or request for legal help (our suggestion, drawing on the types of evidence the legal team lists).

We are a community based in Taiwan. Elsewhere in Asia, who can order content removed and whether a court is involved are settled differently. In Thailand, the urgent procedure in a notification published in July has officials petition a court, with evidence, to suspend dissemination or remove online data.

In Taiwan, Article 46 of the Protection of Children and Youths Welfare and Rights Act requires platforms, once the competent authority notifies them that content is harmful to children, to restrict children's access to it or take it down. The notice goes to the platform, the article sets out no court procedure, and its scope is limited to child protection.

In Hong Kong, Schedule 4 of the Implementation Rules for Article 43 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Safeguarding National Security in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (2020) lets the Commissioner of Police, with the approval of the Secretary for Security, authorise a designated officer to act on electronic messages likely to constitute an offence endangering national security. The officer may require the person who published a message to remove it by a deadline, or require the platform to take a disabling action (removing the message or restricting access to it). If the platform fails to comply or that is not practicable, the requirement can go to a hosting service provider, and failing that, a network service provider. The rules do not require a court first.

Under the same rules, the publisher may receive a removal requirement directly and in writing, but Schedule 4 contains no provision on giving the publisher reasons or a route of appeal. Indonesia's ministerial decree and access cut-off provision let an executive body give orders directly, as in Taiwan and Hong Kong, while Thailand has officials go to a court. The Constitutional Court has now added prior notice with reasons.

When comparing approaches, it helps to ask who can order content removed, whether a court is involved, and whether the person affected receives a notice with reasons and can object. The intended effect of the policy belongs in the comparison too: whether there are published figures to test how well it is curbing disinformation, gambling and pornography.

item.title: Cross-border trade in surveillance technology and export controls
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: An October commentary on Global Voices maps the trade in surveillance technology such as facial recognition and deep packet inspection among Russia, China, Iran, Venezuela and Belarus. International rules on exporting such technology are mostly voluntary or left to each state to enforce. Japan, South Korea and India are Wassenaar participants; mainland China and Taiwan are not. We checked the reports the commentary cites and found several claims worded more broadly than their sources.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 32 sources, including Global Voices Advox, Forbidden Stories, Federal Register

On 15 October, Advox, a project of the international citizen media network Global Voices, published a commentary mapping the trade in surveillance technology among Russia, China, Iran, Venezuela and Belarus. The author, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Bremen in Germany, argues that the greatest danger of AI under authoritarian regimes is that it lets governments suppress protests before they take shape. The author obtained no documents and made no measurements, and most of the commentary's claims link to reports by other media and research institutions. These are deals between states, so ordinary users have no settings to change, and the useful comparison is how different places control exports of surveillance technology.

According to a March report by the investigative journalism organisation Forbidden Stories, the Russian facial recognition company NtechLab licensed an Iranian company as a systems integration partner in 2019, and the software was later sublicensed through Iranian integrators to other buyers. A 2021 contract worth nearly 9 billion rials (about €180,000 at the time) covered real-time facial identification from surveillance cameras, and internal documents cited in the investigation state that both the Revolutionary Guards and the Ministry of Intelligence used the software. None of the companies and agencies Forbidden Stories contacted before publication responded. In December 2024 the US Department of Commerce added NtechLab to its Entity List (exporting controlled US items to a listed company requires a licence first), on the grounds that NtechLab helped the Russian government track peaceful protesters.

A February report by the freedom of expression organisation Article 19 states that ZTE, Huawei, Tiandy and Hikvision continue to operate in Iran despite international sanctions, often through front companies, supplying surveillance technology. The Guardian's coverage of the report carried responses from two of the companies: in February 2026 Hikvision stated that it had left the Iranian market eight years earlier and does not sell there, and ZTE stated that it ceased operations in Iran in 2016. The Guardian article did not carry responses from Huawei or Tiandy, and we did not find any.

The commentary says Protei, a company founded in Russia and headquartered in Jordan, reportedly helped Iran build communications interception and deep packet inspection (DPI, technology that parses the content of each connection in order to filter or monitor it). In 2023 the University of Toronto's Citizen Lab reported, based on leaked documents, that an Iranian mobile virtual network operator had selected Protei to supply core network components including DPI, while noting it had no evidence that final agreements were signed. In November 2025, responding to a report on a hack of the company, the general manager of Protei's Jordan company told TechCrunch that the company has no affiliation with Russia.

The Venezuela and Belarus sections draw on a March report co-authored by the Atlantic Council's Digital Forensic Research Lab (DFRLab) and the local group VE sin Filtro. According to the report, Dahua has kept access to the Venezuelan market despite being added to the US Entity List in 2019 over its involvement in surveillance and repression in Xinjiang. At the time of the listing, Dahua issued a strong protest calling the decision baseless (as carried by Ventas de Seguridad), and we found no response from Dahua to the Venezuela report.

The same report states that Venezuela's interior ministry held talks with the Belarusian company Synesis on facial recognition software between 2021 and 2023, and that it is unknown whether the planned demonstration took place or the software was bought. The US sanctioned Synesis in 2022 for providing software that helped Belarusian authorities identify and arrest protesters. According to a 2021 Biometric Update report, Synesis executives responding to EU sanctions said the company's Kipod system only searches for faces submitted by Belarus's interior ministry and does not identify faces in a crowd.

When we spot-checked the sources the commentary cites, several claims were worded more broadly than their sources. The commentary says up to 80 percent of cameras used in Russia in 2024 were made in China, but the sentence it links to is about the video surveillance market, and the figure is one Russian company's estimate. The commentary cites T-Invariant as saying joint Chinese-Russian development focuses on drones and mass surveillance, but the T-Invariant article it links to does not mention drones or surveillance.

Perspective

Real-time facial recognition matches camera footage against a database of faces, while DPI parses every connection inside a telecom operator's network and decides whether to let it through or block it. Where to draw the line is hard to settle when controlling exports of such technology. According to a law firm's summary of the EU guidelines, commercial items such as billing, marketing and network security are generally excluded, while facial recognition "may" fall under the controls. The guidelines also do not provide an exhaustive product list.

The Digital Silk Road is a digital cooperation framework first proposed by China's National Development and Reform Commission in 2015, which became a foreign policy mechanism in 2017. According to the State Council's summary of a 2023 white paper, China had signed memoranda of understanding on the Digital Silk Road with 17 countries by the end of 2022, and the summary makes no mention of security surveillance. A DFRLab report from February lists exports of AI cameras, facial recognition and predictive policing as part of the "Safe City" model China has promoted heavily, and notes criticism that such technology lacks transparency and effective oversight.

According to the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace's 2019 index, France, Germany, Japan and the United States are also major suppliers of AI surveillance, and 51 percent of advanced democracies deploy AI surveillance systems. These are 2019 figures, and we did not check later changes. The commentary's conclusion also notes that democracies have used surveillance technology to spy on their own citizens.

The Wassenaar Arrangement coordinates export controls on arms and dual-use goods among its members, and as of 29 October it has 42 participating states, including Russia and India but not China. According to the same law firm's summary, the Wassenaar and EU control lists already cover telecommunications interception systems and internet surveillance systems. Decisions are taken by consensus, and each state implements the controls under its own national policies.

The EU's 2021 Dual-Use Regulation brought cyber-surveillance technology that could be used for repression under export controls. The European Commission must report on its evaluation of the regulation between September 2026 and September 2028, and the public consultation closed on 15 October. The UK and France launched the Pall Mall Process in 2024 and in April 2025 published a voluntary, non-binding code of practice for states that covers only commercial cyber intrusion tools such as spyware and intrusion services. Facial recognition and smart cities fall outside its scope, and the 27 supporting states listed on the UK government page include Japan and South Korea.

Taiwan is not a Wassenaar participant, and we could not find out whether its export licensing covers surveillance items. On the use side, Article 11 of the Cyber Security Management Act, as amended in 2025, bars government agencies from using products harmful to national cyber security, meaning systems, services or products that the competent authority has determined pose such a risk. The Regulations for the Review of Products Harmful to National Cyber Security, issued by the Ministry of Digital Affairs as competent authority in December 2025, add that when a reported product is of a Mainland China brand, the ministry may proceed directly to cyber security information sharing.

The regulations name no vendors, and we could not find on official pages whether Hikvision or Dahua fall within their scope. Article 11 applies only to government agencies and does not cover businesses or members of the public using cameras from these brands.

Across Asia, participation in the Wassenaar Arrangement and the Pall Mall code varies. Japan, South Korea and India are among the 42 Wassenaar participants, while mainland China and Taiwan are not. On commercial intrusion tools, Japan and South Korea are among the 27 supporting states of the Pall Mall code, and India, Taiwan and mainland China are not on the list.

Rules on how police use facial recognition differ as well. South Korea's Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and the Establishment of Trust, in force since 22 January 2026, classes as high-impact AI those AI systems that may significantly affect life, bodily safety or fundamental rights and are used in listed areas, one of which is analysing biometric data such as faces for criminal investigations or arrests. AI business operators, which the act defines to include state agencies, owe risk management, explanation, user protection, human oversight and record-keeping duties when they provide high-impact AI. We did not check whether police using such a system count as an AI business operator under the act.

We, a community based in Taiwan, found no law in Taiwan that expressly regulates police use of facial recognition matching, though we searched only the Police Power Exercise Act and the Personal Data Protection Act. In Japan, police photograph arrested suspects and the photos are kept by the National Police Agency under the National Public Safety Commission's Rules on the Management and Use of Suspect Photographs, which make no mention of facial recognition or matching. Police officials told the Diet in 2021 that, in individual cases, police match suspects' facial images from security cameras against suspect photos the police hold, and we found no law or National Public Safety Commission rule that expressly regulates this matching. In mainland China, the Measures for the Security Management of Facial Recognition Technology Applications, in force since 1 June 2025, require facial recognition devices in public places to be necessary for maintaining public security and clearly signposted, though the text does not say whether they apply in practice to systems run by public security authorities.

The use-side rules in South Korea and Taiwan attach to different things. South Korea's statute attaches duties to providers of AI used in criminal investigations, while the Taiwanese rule we found attaches to which products government agencies may use. In neither place did we establish whether police use of facial recognition itself is covered.

For the state of internet freedom and surveillance in a given country, Freedom House publishes Freedom on the Net country reports every year (the 2025 edition covers 72 countries).

To compare approaches across places, readers can ask whether exporting surveillance technology requires a licence, whether licensing reviews assess human rights, and whether buyer countries have laws regulating facial recognition and public surveillance cameras. Whether the controls achieve what they set out to do matters too. The Article 19 report describes vendors operating through front companies under sanctions, and the DFRLab report describes Dahua keeping its Venezuelan market after being listed. As of 29 October, we had found no systematic study evaluating how effective these controls are.

item.title: The effectiveness of Iran's internet filtering and the government's countermeasures against Starlink
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: According to an October report by Filterwatch, a group that monitors Iran's internet, Iran's government fears its filtering is failing against satellite internet and has turned to signal jamming, equipment confiscation and diplomatic pressure. The secretary of the Supreme Council of Cyberspace claims Iran can already disable Starlink terminals, while the CEO of the Telecommunication Infrastructure Company, who is also a deputy minister of communications, said the ministry's official position is that current filtering policy has not been effective. Under a 2025 law, individuals who use unlicensed satellite internet equipment face imprisonment.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 18 sources, including Filterwatch, Zoomit, Tehran Times

Iran's government fears that its filtering is becoming ineffective against satellite internet, according to a report published on 14 October by Filterwatch, a group that monitors Iran's internet (launched in 2012 by Small Media, a London-based digital rights organisation, and now part of the Miaan Group). In the report's analysis, ordinary filtering is applied on domestic operators' networks and at international gateways. Starlink terminals connect directly to satellites, so their traffic passes through neither. The government's response has therefore shifted to jamming signals, confiscating equipment, punishing users and applying diplomatic pressure, and the penalties and jamming both apply inside Iran.

The Iranian technology outlet Zoomit reported that on 5 October the secretary of the Supreme Council of Cyberspace claimed Iran had disabled Starlink terminals "in a controlled manner" during the unrest of the Iranian month of Dey (roughly late December 2025 to mid-January 2026) and the nationwide shutdown in January. The secretary cited reports on Western websites in support and said Iran had other technologies available. The day before, Iran's foreign ministry summoned Norway's ambassador to protest that Norway had not acted on decisions of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) Radio Regulations Board to stop unauthorised Starlink transmissions inside Iran.

Iranian officials do not agree on how well the measures work. According to the semi-official Mehr News Agency on 14 September, the CEO of the Telecommunication Infrastructure Company, who is also a deputy minister of communications, said the ministry's official position is that current filtering policy has not been effective, and that decisions do not rest with a single ministry. The CEO estimated Starlink traffic in Iran at about 1 Tbps (one terabit per second), still a low share of national traffic, and said domestic institutions had no precise user figures. The CEO also said international traffic had returned to about 90% of its earlier level.

The technology outlet Digiato relayed a warning from another deputy minister of communications that continued restrictive policies push users towards tools that do not depend on the domestic network. Gadgetnews and Digiato also quoted this deputy minister telling a meeting that, on current trends, the next crisis would leave no option but to cut the power, because Starlink no longer depends on Iran's network.

In 2025 Iran passed the Law on Intensifying Punishment for Espionage and Cooperation with the Israeli Regime and Hostile States against National Security and Interests, which cleared the Guardian Council in October that year. Under Article 5, as relayed by Hamshahri Online, using, carrying, keeping, buying, selling or importing unlicensed satellite internet equipment such as Starlink for personal use is punishable by a grade 6 prison term and confiscation of the equipment (reports differ on the length of the term). Supply, production, distribution and installation carry a grade 5 prison term, and the death penalty applies where the purpose is to oppose the system or to spy and the offender is regarded as a hostile force. As of 29 October we had found no prosecution under this article.

Perspective

The deputy minister quoted by Digiato also said that if direct-to-cell technology, which connects phones straight to satellites, becomes widespread, even mobile device registration (the government's most basic means of verifying identity) will stop working. According to Tehran Times' account of the secretary of the Supreme Council of Cyberspace, about 80% of Starlink packets were disrupted during the unrest, and most of the remaining traffic became largely ineffective. The secretary also cited Starlink's use in conflicts such as Ukraine, saying satellite communications can support military command and intelligence gathering.

A NasNet technician interviewed by Filterwatch (the report links NasNet to the website of a router configuration tool built around Starlink connections) said packet loss in some areas reached about 80% in January and fell to about 10% after Starlink updates. The technician also said Iran had never managed to disable Starlink completely across the country. In its key findings, Filterwatch cites technical assessments that a nationwide shutdown is not technically feasible, and in the body of the report the basis is this technician's account. The technician was describing packet loss and the secretary the share of packets disrupted, so the two 80% figures may not measure the same thing (our assessment).

Under Article 18 of the ITU Radio Regulations and related resolutions, a transmitting earth station needs authorisation from the administration of the country where it operates. According to the Board's page on the ITU website, in March the Board found that the actions of Norway, the notifying administration for the Starlink system, did not comply with its obligations, but that the Board had no authority to suspend the system's frequency assignments on those grounds. At its 102nd meeting, from late June to early July, the Board strongly urged Norway and the United States to have the operator immediately stop unauthorised transmissions inside Iran, and asked Iran to make every effort to identify and deactivate unauthorised terminals on its territory.

On the same page, the Board summarises Norway's position that it would not enforce the Board's earlier decisions without an explicit requirement in the regulatory framework, and the United States' view that the Board was exceeding its mandate under the ITU Constitution. The Board's 103rd meeting runs from 26 to 30 October, and as of 29 October we could find no outcome. According to Tehran Times, citing Iran's foreign ministry, the Iranian official who summoned the Norwegian ambassador referred to the United States and Israel using Starlink to support interventionist activities against Iran. This is the Iranian government's account, which we have not independently verified, and we found no public response from SpaceX or the Norwegian government to the summons.

Cloudflare Radar recorded a traffic anomaly in HTTP requests from Iran on 4 October, after which daily peaks were around 40% of the high on the evening of 3 October, recovering day by day to 60 to 70% on 17 to 19 October (rough readings from our query on 29 October). Filterwatch notes user reports of VPN failures in the same period and puts forward a hypothesis of interference aimed at circumvention tools. According to Filterwatch's account, which links to a post on X, the director of internet analysis at the network analytics company Kentik confirmed that the drop was limited to Cloudflare's network, and told Filterwatch that Iran's overall traffic was about 60% of its level before 8 January (the country was under a nationwide shutdown in January). Filterwatch considers this inconsistent with the 90% figure the CEO gave on 14 September, though the two may rest on different baselines and measures (our inference).

In another report from the same period, Filterwatch analyses three Android malware cases, each starting with a Telegram message. One of the apps was disguised as a Starlink and VPN tool. According to the report, a critical part of each operation was persuading the target to install an app from outside an official app store. A message from a friend's account may indicate that the account was compromised, but the evidence is insufficient to confirm it.

We are a community based in Taiwan, where the recent legislative change concerns operators. According to Business Today, the amendment to Article 36 of the Telecommunications Management Act, which passed its third reading in the Legislative Yuan on 21 July, covers operators setting up public telecommunications networks with satellite technology. Once the competent authority has considered national security and other factors and given approval, such operators can be exempted from limits including the cap on foreign shareholding. We could not find rules on individuals owning or using terminals, nor, as of 29 October, whether SpaceX has applied; during the committee review, the Minister of Digital Affairs relayed that Starlink had told the government it was not especially interested in the Taiwan market.

In South Korea, The Asia Business Daily reported in August 2025 that, according to the Ministry of Science and ICT, a SpaceX earth station terminal had passed conformity assessment, after which each company could decide when to launch. In December 2025 Korea JoongAng Daily reported residential and business plans on the Starlink Korea website with preregistration open, and named KT SAT and SK Telink as licensed resellers on the enterprise side. Both are press reports, and we did not find the ministry's own announcement. Beyond the equipment assessment, we found no rules on whether individuals need a separate permit to own or use a terminal.

In India, according to Advanced Television in June 2026, the Department of Telecommunications granted Starlink a Unified License with authorisation for Global Mobile Personal Communication by Satellite services in June 2025, while SpaceX said it had received a letter of intent and the final licence had yet to be granted. We found no rules on individuals owning or using terminals in India.

Advanced Television also summarised a Bloomberg report linking the delay to Iran, according to which the Ministry of Home Affairs had withheld final clearances amid concerns that grew after reports of Starlink terminals operating in Iran, where the service is not licensed. Officials were said to be examining whether the company could meet Indian security requirements when facing competing demands from foreign governments. A Starlink vice president called the report misleading and said discussions with the government were continuing. We found nothing on developments after June.

In mainland China, the rules and enforcement we found concern ships. According to the trade publication The Maritime Executive in January, China's Maritime Traffic Safety Law requires vessels under Chinese jurisdiction to route digital communications through coast stations or satellite gateway stations licensed by the authorities, and Starlink is not among the approved operators. Fines reach 100,000 yuan in serious cases, and up to 500,000 yuan under separate radio regulations when the equipment is used for illegal activities.

Citing the P&I correspondent Oasis, The Maritime Executive also reported that the maritime safety administration for the port of Ningbo opened the first known inquiry into a vessel's connectivity in December 2025. In a notice on 9 January, the P&I club Steamship Mutual wrote that Chinese authorities had recently started to penalise vessels for using Starlink within Chinese jurisdictional waters. These are industry summaries. We did not check the original legal texts, and found no rules or cases on individuals holding or using terminals on land.

Readers outside Iran do not need to change their habits because of this news. Filterwatch analysed Android cases, and the tactic of steering targets to install apps from outside official stores could appear elsewhere, so links and installation files sent by friends are not necessarily trustworthy (our inference).

One way to compare approaches is to ask who approves satellite internet operators and whether individuals need permission to own a terminal. On the first point, Taiwan lets satellite operators be exempted from foreign-ownership limits after case-by-case approval, the reported step in South Korea was a conformity assessment of a terminal model, India's final clearance has reportedly been held up in a security review (which Starlink disputes), and in mainland China ships must route traffic through licensed stations. On the second point, we found no rules for individuals in any of the four places.

When a government asks an operator to disable terminals on its territory, whether it relies on domestic law, ITU rules or the operator's terms of service is another point of difference. The comparison should also cover what a policy is meant to achieve, including whether independent measurements exist to check official claims about how well filtering and shutdowns work.

item.title: Dispute over the UK Home Office's use of generative AI to summarise asylum interviews
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: In October, the UK digital rights group Open Rights Group published an investigation into two generative AI tools the Home Office uses in asylum cases, one of which summarises interview transcripts. Home Office subject matter experts checked 203 summaries and judged 22% unusable in the first round. The minister responsible for asylum wrote in an August letter that applicants are not specifically told AI was involved in handling their claims. According to the Home Office, the tools only assist and do not replace caseworkers' decisions.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 20 sources, including Open Rights Group, Home Office, Home Office (published by Open Rights Group)

On 12 October, the UK digital rights group Open Rights Group (ORG) published a report pulling together six months of investigation into two generative AI tools used by the Home Office. The Asylum Case Summarisation (ACS) tool turns asylum interview transcripts into summaries for decision-makers, and the Asylum Policy Search (APS) tool lets decision-makers search country policy information through a chat-style interface. ORG's report gives OpenAI's GPT-4o as the model behind both, provided through Microsoft's Azure. ORG's January paper and WIRED give GPT-4 instead, and the Home Office's own public documents do not name the model.

ACS was fully rolled out in April 2026. Based on material ORG obtained through parliamentary questions and freedom of information requests, Home Office subject matter experts have since checked 203 summaries. In the first round, 45 were judged unusable (22%), and another 19 were flagged and sent for a second-round review. Of 56 summaries reviewed in the second round, 30 were unusable, which the report counts as 15% using 203 as the denominator (30÷203 is about 14.8%, by our calculation), and the report does not explain why the 19 and the 56 do not match.

ORG compares these two figures with the 9% in the Home Office's 2025 pilot evaluation. That figure was the share of summaries removed for inaccuracy or missing information after technical specialists reviewed every summary during the pilot, a different method from the sampling after roll-out. The Register reported that the Home Office did not respond to its questions, and we found no public Home Office response to these figures.

Using monthly averages from the data protection impact assessment (the assessment required before processing high-risk personal data), ORG estimates that about 70,000 cases were processed between April and July, of which only 0.3% were checked by experts. The people affected are those applying for asylum in the UK, and in August the minister responsible for asylum wrote to an MP that applicants are not specifically told AI has been used in the consideration of their claims. The Home Office's privacy notice states that parts of the processing may involve automation and that complex or adverse decisions are always taken by trained staff, with no mention of the two tools. In a legal opinion commissioned by ORG and signed in February (an opinion obtained by the commissioning party and not tested in court), three lawyers concluded that not telling applicants is "likely to be unlawful", and we found no public Home Office response to the opinion.

Perspective

In the Home Office response quoted by WIRED, asylum decisions are made by trained caseworkers, and the tools cannot be used in isolation and do not make decisions on claims. The previous minister's June letter adds that the summary is only one of the documents decision-makers read before deciding, and that they must still read all documents in the case. The Home Office has also committed to publishing updated evaluations.

The 2025 pilot evaluation found that the group using ACS reviewed a transcript 23 minutes faster than the comparison group (a saving of about 32%). By the evaluation's own account, these were small-scale pilots and further evaluation would be needed before a full roll-out. ORG argues that if decision-makers still have to read every document, those time savings cannot be achieved.

Using figures obtained through freedom of information requests, ORG reports that since April 2026 the monthly number of initial substantive decisions has fallen by about 42% compared with the same period a year earlier, and the mean time from interview to decision has risen by 29%. The Register's report notes that these figures do not prove AI caused the change, and that they show little sign of the productivity gains ministers promised. ORG calls for an outright ban on AI in asylum applications, and its report recommends first suspending both tools and commissioning an independent audit.

The two sides describe what the tools do differently. The minister's August letter states that the tools summarise information provided by the claimant and do not generate new content. ORG's report, by contrast, describes both tools as generating new text that can filter, reframe or omit facts relevant to a decision.

ORG's report describes a large language model's summary as newly generated sentences, and the minister's August letter does not explain what "new content" covers. In the pilot evaluation, ACS summaries deliberately did not mark where each point came from in the transcript, to reduce the pilot's technical complexity, and this could be revisited later. Without reference numbers, decision-makers cannot easily check a summary against the original wording of the transcript (our inference), and adding reference numbers to the summaries is among the plans in the minister's letter.

The previous minister's June letter states that experts dip-sample ACS output every week, and the Home Office also told WIRED that it regularly monitors the tools' performance. In ORG's report, the sampling form scores whether a summary omits the most relevant facts, but that criterion is not one of the conditions for failing a summary. On that basis, ORG considers that a summary missing important facts could still pass as long as the rest is accurate, and we have not seen a Home Office explanation of the scoring criteria.

Whether applicants can see the summaries is a separate question. ORG's report states that applicants cannot see or correct the AI summaries of their own interviews. The minister's August letter mentions that applicants can amend the interview record within an agreed period after the interview, and that ACS is used after that period to help decision-makers re-familiarise themselves with the case, but the letter does not say whether applicants can see or correct the summaries.

The UK government runs a set of transparency records through which public bodies publish their algorithmic tools (Algorithmic Transparency Records). When we checked on 29 October there were 154 records, and neither of the Home Office's two is for these tools. The minister's letter explains that both tools were developed before these records became mandatory, and their records are now being completed. ORG's request for the prompts used by the tools was refused, partly on cyber security grounds, and the equality impact assessment (a document assessing a policy's effects on different groups), which the minister said would be published in August, was still unpublished as of 12 October.

In June, the Independent Chief Inspector of Borders and Immigration, who oversees the Home Office's border and immigration functions, published an inspection of asylum casework from June to December 2025, finding that the effectiveness and reliability of APS were varied. In the inspection report, inspectors also found evidence of AI tools being used inappropriately in decision letters and interviews, including Microsoft's AI assistant Copilot, which the Home Office does not permit in asylum interviews and decision-making, and ChatGPT. Managers of the asylum decision-making units told inspectors that these instances had been addressed. WIRED reports that the inspectorate asked ORG for more information to help set next year's inspection topics, but stated that it cannot confirm which topics are under consideration before they are published.

With interview records processed in Azure, who might read an applicant's account depends on the terms of the service (our inference). Microsoft's documentation states that customers' prompts (the text sent to the model) and outputs are not available to OpenAI and are not used to improve the models. The service still runs abuse monitoring to detect misuse, under which prompts and outputs flagged by the system may be reviewed by authorised Microsoft employees, while customers approved for modified abuse monitoring are exempt from this storage and human review.

Microsoft's documentation also lists several deployment types with different data processing locations, and prompts and responses for the Global type may be processed in any geography where the model is deployed. As of 29 October, we could find no explanation from the Home Office itself of which deployment type it uses or whether it has modified abuse monitoring.

Taiwan's Executive Yuan (Taiwan's cabinet) issued its reference guidelines on the use of generative AI by the Executive Yuan and its subordinate agencies (行政院及所屬機關（構）使用生成式AI參考指引) in 2023. They apply to the Executive Yuan and its agencies and are framed as reference guidelines. Under item 5, agencies may not use unverified output to take administrative action directly or as the sole basis for an official decision, which is close to the Home Office's position that the tools cannot be used in isolation. Under item 6, agencies should make appropriate disclosure when using generative AI as an assistive tool, with no wording on to whom, whereas the UK minister's letter states that applicants are not specifically told.

Under Article 19 of Taiwan's AI Basic Act (人工智慧基本法), promulgated in January 2026, the government must also carry out a risk assessment when using AI in its work. We, a community based in Taiwan, found no rule in Taiwan specific to the use of AI in immigration or asylum procedures.

South Korea draws the line in statute rather than in guidance, and under Article 20 of the General Act on Public Administration, an administrative authority may impose a disposition using a fully automated system, including systems that employ AI, except for dispositions imposed at its discretion. We read the article in the English translation by the Korea Legislation Research Institute and did not check the Korean original, which secondary sources describe as adding wording to the effect of "as prescribed by statute". We have not read the primary text of Article 37-2 of Korea's Personal Information Protection Act, the provision on automated decisions, so whether Korean law requires telling the person affected that AI was involved remains unverified. We found no provision specific to asylum procedures.

In mainland China, the Guidelines for the Deployment and Application of Large AI Models in Government Affairs were issued by the Office of the Central Cyberspace Affairs Commission and the National Development and Reform Commission, and published on the Cyberspace Administration of China's website on 10 October 2025. The opening of the guidelines describes them as providing orientation and a basic reference for government departments at all levels. Under the guidelines, large models are to stay in an "assistive" role, and applications must display a risk warning in a prominent place on the interface, state the service's limitations and label model output, which is aimed at people using the interface rather than at those affected by a decision. The guidelines contain no wording against using model output as the sole basis for a decision.

China's Personal Information Protection Law applies to state organs under Article 33, and under Article 24, individuals may ask for an explanation of a decision made through automated decision-making that significantly affects their rights and interests, and may refuse a decision made solely by automated means. The provision covers automated decision-making in general and does not mention generative AI, and we did not look into how state organs apply it in practice. Under Article 36, personal information handled by state organs must be stored within China, with a security assessment required if it genuinely needs to be provided abroad. We found no rule in mainland China specific to the use of generative AI in asylum or immigration reviews.

Japan's guideline on the procurement and use of generative AI in government (DS-920), decided in May 2025 by the executive board of the Digital Society Promotion Council, is labelled "Normative", a set of rules to be complied with in developing and managing government information systems. The guideline contains no explicit ban on relying solely on AI output and handles the issue through risk assessment instead. Each ministry's Chief AI Officer uses a high-risk assessment sheet on which work with a major effect on people's fundamental rights or safety, and output used without a government employee's judgement, both raise the risk level, and cases judged high-risk must be reported to an advisory board on advanced AI use.

We found no provision in the guideline on telling people affected by an administrative decision that AI was involved. The provisions above are from the first edition of May 2025. A version 2.0 was adopted in June 2026 according to press reports, and we have not read it.

People dealing with agencies under Taiwan's Executive Yuan can ask the agency handling their case whether generative AI is used on it (our suggestion). Item 6 contains no wording on to whom disclosure is owed or how much must be disclosed, so asking does not guarantee a complete answer. Beyond that, readers do not need to change their habits because of this.

When comparing how governments use AI on individual cases, readers can look at whether the people concerned are told, whether they can see and correct what the AI produced, whether the sampling rate and criteria are published, and whether omitted facts count as errors. The intended effect of the policy matters too, including whether the time saved outweighs the cost of errors, who carries out the evaluation, and whether the results are published.
