item.title: The lawsuit to revoke Thailand's notification on urgent takedowns of online content
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: In July, Thailand's Ministry of Digital Economy and Society published a notification defining the online data that may be the subject of an urgent court petition for suspension or removal under the Computer Crime Act, including 14 categories contrary to public order or good morals. On 14 October, Thai Lawyers for Human Rights and iLaw asked the Central Administrative Court to revoke the definition of "urgent necessity" and the two categories on the monarchy and on hatred. As of 29 October, the ministry's explanations had cited only examples such as scams and e-cigarette advertising, and we found no response on the two categories or the lawsuit.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 13 sources, including ราชกิจจานุเบกษา, ศูนย์ทนายความเพื่อสิทธิมนุษยชน, iLaw

Thai Lawyers for Human Rights (TLHR) and iLaw filed a suit at the Central Administrative Court on 14 October, asking it to revoke parts of a notification issued by the Ministry of Digital Economy and Society (MDES). The notification was signed on 19 June, published in the Royal Gazette on 17 July and took effect the next day. It defines "urgent necessity" under Section 20 of the Computer Crime Act as a situation in which delay could threaten national security, religion, the monarchy, good morals, social culture or public order, and provides that in such cases an official designated within the ministry petitions a court, with evidence, to suspend the dissemination of the data or remove it. According to TLHR's summary, paragraph 5 of Section 20 lets officials petition a court in urgent cases before the minister or the Computer Data Screening Committee has approved.

Under the definition sit four types of data. The fourth is a list of 14 categories contrary to public order or good morals, covering any data that falls into them and has been approved by the Computer Data Screening Committee. The categories include gambling, sales of illegal firearms, e-cigarettes, cannabis, alcohol, lending above the legal interest rate, surrogacy advertising, and images or text that mock, ridicule, belittle or refer to Buddhism in a way that damages it or exposes it to abuse or hatred.

The lawsuit targets only two of these categories, along with the definition of "urgent necessity" itself. One covers content that defames, ridicules, refers to or belittles the King, the Queen, the Heir-Apparent, the Regent, members of the royal family or the monarchy. The other covers images or text that demean others and incite hatred, create a sense of division or negative stereotypes, and could lead to social division, conflict and wider violence.

According to a Daily News report of 21 July, the ministry's permanent secretary said the notification removed time constraints in the previous screening process. Illegal URLs had grown from tens of thousands to millions, and handling time could fall from several days to a few hours. The scope covers all kinds of online threats, such as mule accounts, deepfake investment scams, e-cigarette advertising and SMS scams. Ministry figures show 883,012 URLs blocked from October 2025 to 13 July 2026, before the notification took effect.

In July, the law firm Tilleke & Gibbins advised platforms, e-commerce businesses and fintech companies to expect a significant increase in government-initiated takedown orders.

Perspective

The notification governs online data disseminated in Thailand, so those directly affected are people who publish or access content in Thailand, and the platforms and internet service providers that must comply with court orders. We found no explanation of how it treats posts made outside Thailand. The points in dispute were raised by the plaintiffs, and as of 29 October the ministry had not responded publicly to any of them or to the lawsuit itself.

The first point is the minister's authority. The notification was issued, according to its text, under Section 4 of the Computer Crime Act, and the reason given in its preamble is a large increase in illegal or inappropriate data that calls for a stronger mechanism to stop its dissemination. TLHR argues that Section 4 only authorises the minister to set procedures and mechanisms for carrying out the act, and gives no power to define "urgent necessity" under paragraph 5 of Section 20.

The second point is scope and wording. The clause on the monarchy includes a reason for listing it, namely that these figures are revered by the people according to the beliefs and traditions of Thai society. TLHR argues that the categories go beyond what Section 20 sets out, and that "refer to", which the Royal Institute dictionary defines as "to be connected with", could also capture neutral mentions. TLHR also notes that "the monarchy" is not defined in law, while the ministry's July explanations discussed only scams, gambling, e-cigarette advertising and URL counts.

In an analysis from July, iLaw notes that Section 112 of the Criminal Code, the lèse-majesté provision, protects the King, the Queen, the Heir-Apparent and the Regent. The notification extends the list to members of the royal family and adds "refer to" to the covered acts. iLaw also argues that the category on hatred leaves officials and the screening committee room for discretion that could take in good-faith criticism, while noting that most categories are acts already prohibited under other laws.

The third point is procedure. Clauses 3 and 4 of the notification set out how a petition is filed: an official submits evidence to a court, and must strictly follow the relevant laws and regulations. TLHR and iLaw further argue that the ministry did not hold the consultation required by law before issuing it, and iLaw found no consultation on the ministry's website or on the government's central law portal.

A second suit reached the same court on the same day. According to MGR Online, another foundation also asked for the notification to be revoked, arguing that it could make people censor themselves out of fear. As of 29 October, TLHR, iLaw and the press had reported only the filing, and we found nothing on whether the court has accepted either case or issued any stay.

Beyond the lawsuit, the permanent secretary's explanation and the text of the notification differ on one point. In the explanation, the fast-track process involves working with foreign social media platforms and Thai internet service providers to stop content directly, without waiting for a court order, when it is clearly illegal. The notification contains no such provision. The Nation, an English-language Thai newspaper, also reports that the ministry's existing procedure under Section 14 of the Computer Crime Act lets officials, with the approval of the permanent secretary or a designated deputy, order providers to suspend or remove certain illegal computer data.

We are a community based in Taiwan, where "good morals" appears in Article 72 of the Civil Code, which concerns whether a juridical act is valid and is not a standard for taking down online content.

As far as we found in Taiwan's statutes, the closest mechanism for harmful content is in the Protection of Children and Youths Welfare and Rights Act, last amended in January 2021 according to the Laws and Regulations Database. Article 43 lists the categories, and under Article 46 complaints go to iWIN (Institute of Watch Internet Network). When the competent authority notifies a platform that content is harmful to children's physical or mental health, the platform must restrict children's access to it or remove it first. That mechanism does not go through a court, and it protects only children and young people.

In mainland China, Article 4 of the Provisions on the Governance of the Online Information Content Ecosystem, issued by the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) and in force since 1 March 2020, requires producers of online information content to obey laws and regulations and to "follow public order and good customs" (遵循公序良俗). The specific categories come in two tiers, in Articles 6 and 7.

Article 6 lists 11 kinds of illegal information that producers may not create, copy or publish, including content spreading obscenity, pornography, gambling or violence, inciting ethnic hatred or discrimination, undermining the state's religious policy, or harming national honour and interests. Article 7 adds nine kinds of negative information that producers must "take measures to prevent and resist", such as sexually suggestive content and content inciting discrimination against groups or regions. The last of the nine is "other content that has an adverse effect on the online ecosystem", with no specific conduct named.

Under Article 10, platforms may not disseminate the information in Article 6 and must prevent and resist disseminating the information in Article 7. On finding either, they must immediately take measures in accordance with the law, keep records and report to the competent authorities. We searched the full text of the Provisions and found no occurrence of "court" (法院); the duty to act falls directly on platforms, whereas the Thai notification requires officials to petition a court.

Readers can compare approaches across jurisdictions with a few questions. First, whether the categories of content that may be restricted are written into statute or filled in by an administrative notification or regulation. Second, whether suspending dissemination requires a court first, and whether cooperation with platforms outside the courts follows published rules. Third, whether an urgent procedure can deal within hours with clearly illegal content such as scams, and whether categories concerning speech should be handled separately from it.

item.title: The European Data Protection Board's preliminary guidance on smart glasses
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: On 13 October the European Data Protection Board adopted a statement on smart glasses, noting that because they look much like ordinary glasses, people nearby may be filmed or recorded without knowing it. The statement recommends that manufacturers signal recording with reliable lights and sounds that are hard to switch off, and that recording should not be possible while the light is covered. The press release presents the statement as preliminary guidance, and the statement sets no new rules and names no manufacturer.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 19 sources, including European Data Protection Board, netzpolitik.org, Privacy Guides

On 13 October the European Data Protection Board (EDPB, the body made up of the data protection authorities of the EU member states) adopted a statement on smart glasses, setting out under the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) the responsibilities of users, manufacturers and service providers in the EU. According to the statement, smart glasses bring new uses for communication and assistance, such as real-time translation and support for people with visual impairments.

According to the statement, these glasses look much like ordinary glasses, so collecting and recording personal data is barely noticeable. Microphones on some models can pick up background conversations the wearer is not part of. The statement adds that combining smart glasses with face or voice recognition systems poses a high risk to rights and freedoms in public spaces.

Users who record only for a purely personal or household activity, such as sharing only with family or friends, are not subject to the GDPR. The statement says this exemption must be narrowly construed, and other laws, such as criminal law, may still apply. Users who share to a public social media account or use the glasses at work become controllers (the party that decides the purpose and means of processing). Manufacturers and providers of AI features are also controllers where they decide the purposes and means, and the statement says they should not rely on users to meet their duty to inform people nearby.

For manufacturers, the statement recommends combining several signals. A light should be visible in many lighting conditions, recording should not be possible while the light is covered, and a shutter sound can be added. Phone notifications that detect nearby glasses can help but should not be the only signal, and should not allow the wearer to be tracked. The EDPB's press release presents the statement as preliminary guidance; the statement itself sets no new rules, names no manufacturer and closes by saying the EDPB will continue to analyse the privacy concerns smart glasses raise.

Perspective

The light is the main cue people nearby have that they are being filmed. We could not reach Meta's own website, so Meta's statements here come from its newsroom post as quoted by Privacy Guides and 9to5Google. Every pair has a white capture LED on the front that blinks briefly for a photo and keeps blinking during video, and the LED has no off switch. From the second generation onwards, the camera is disabled when the glasses detect that the LED is blocked, and a July update also disables the camera if the LED has been tampered with or destroyed.

According to PPC Land's paraphrase, Meta considers a shutter sound impractical for notifying people at a distance and points to precedents such as laptop camera indicators for its use of a light.

In September the data protection authority of Hamburg in Germany published an inspection report on Ray-Ban Meta, and as netzpolitik.org reports it, the report's conclusion is that the LED is only of limited visibility depending on distance, angle and lighting. CORRECTIV reports two further findings. Blocking is checked only when recording starts, so covering the light mid-recording does not stop it, and on the second generation the light stays off entirely while AI features are in use (netzpolitik.org only mentions an inspection of the first generation). A footnote in the EDPB statement adds that a white LED could be mistaken for a reflection.

Section 8 of Germany's Telecommunications Digital Services Data Protection Act (TDDDG) bans devices disguised as everyday objects and designed for covert audio or video recording, and the Federal Network Agency (Bundesnetzagentur) is the responsible authority. Asked by CORRECTIV, the agency assessed the LED as clearly recognisable within 5 metres and found the conditions for a ban not currently met. The agency also said that the mere possibility of modification is no reason for a ban, and that it had not yet examined the second generation.

TNW reported that a Meta executive announced on Threads on 27 August an update that stops the camera when the light is covered, and described it as closing the gap of starting a recording and then covering the light. That is TNW's account. The report does not say which firmware version Hamburg inspected, and we cannot confirm that the two refer to the same gap.

In October, users reported that Ray-Ban Meta glasses had saved recordings of conversations without the wake word being spoken. Meta's response to Android Authority, as quoted by Privacy Guides, says the issue has been resolved and that users can manage, review and delete their voice recordings in settings at any time. As of 29 October, none of the reports we read gave the cause or the number of people affected. The reports we read also mention only voice recordings, not photos or videos.

Ray-Ban Meta wearers concerned about accidental recording can review and delete voice recordings in the glasses' privacy settings in the Meta AI app. According to TechRadar, deletion only works after the fact and cannot prevent capture. TechRadar also writes that turning off voice activation seems to stop the problem, while ChannelNews notes that the cost is losing hands-free access to the assistant, which can still be called up with the button.

France's data protection authority, CNIL, also has recommendations for wearers. CNIL advises telling people nearby, switching off capture features when not needed and turning off the glasses wherever people are asked to turn off their phones, and suggests getting consent before posting images that show other people on social media.

People being filmed have fewer options. CNIL's page says lights that inform people nearby have only limited effect and are absent for some uses, and the EDPB statement says phone apps that detect smart glasses can only tell that glasses are nearby, not whether they are recording. If it matters to you, the simplest step is to ask the wearer directly whether they are recording (our suggestion).

Singapore's Ministry of Digital Development and Information (MDDI) answered two parliamentary questions on smart glasses in 2026. In its 8 April answer, the ministry wrote that smart glasses with AI capabilities "are subject to existing safeguards for data protection and safety in Singapore". Organisations offering them must comply with the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA), and an organisation that transfers such data to third-party contractors overseas remains responsible for protection comparable to Singapore's standards.

Asked on 6 May whether it would introduce visual indicator requirements, the ministry replied that photography and recording are "subject to the same rules and principles regardless of the form factor of the device". According to the answer, organisations, including individuals creating content for commercial purposes, are accountable under the PDPA, which generally does not require them to seek consent for photography or recording in public spaces, but they must ensure that any later use or disclosure of the data, including for AI features, is for a reasonable purpose. The answer announced no indicator requirement. Both answers state that non-consensual recording, sharing or other misuse of intimate or private content may be a criminal offence under the Penal Code and the Protection from Harassment Act.

In South Korea, the news agency Newsis reported on 3 August that, according to the Personal Information Protection Commission (PIPC), the commission met Samsung staff in late July about the AI glasses Samsung plans to release within the year. They discussed notification devices, such as a light or sound, that make it easy for people nearby to notice when the camera and microphone are in use. The PIPC had earlier met Meta, which has launched its AI glasses in South Korea, and the report says the government plans to draw up privacy principles for AI glasses and autonomous robots with industry in the second half of 2026. We did not obtain a PIPC press release, so this account rests on the Newsis report.

As of 29 October, we found no statement or guidance specifically on smart glasses from Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC). A compendium of the approaches of G7 data protection authorities, compiled by CNIL in 2026, summarises earlier PPC recommendations on camera systems with face identification, and the compendium lists the PPC's view that camera images can fall within the scope of the Act on the Protection of Personal Information if they can identify a specific individual.

We, a community based in Taiwan, found no rules in Taiwan specific to smart glasses and no explanation from the authorities as of 29 October. Article 315-1 of Taiwan's Criminal Code punishes recording another person's non-public activities, speech or conversations without lawful reason, where non-public means not open to others, so that people do not expect to be heard or seen. We did not find the original text of any court rulings on whether filming in a public place counts as non-public.

Article 51 of the Personal Data Protection Act of Taiwan excludes purely personal or household activities, as well as audio-visual material collected in public places or at public events that is not combined with other personal data. Going by the wording, our reading is that footage combined with other personal data, for example when AI is used to identify who someone is, falls outside that exclusion.

Readers can compare approaches with a few questions. One is whether, when people nearby are filmed, the law looks only at whether the place is public or also at how the footage is used afterwards, as Singapore's answer does for organisations. Hamburg and the Federal Network Agency reached different conclusions on how visible the light is, after examining different models in different situations, so it is also worth comparing who should carry out such tests and against what standard, and whether indicator requirements belong in law or in agreements with industry. It is also worth comparing how each place's rules preserve features that help users, such as assistance for people with visual impairments and real-time translation.

item.title: SSH login interception through compromised Tor exit relays
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: In early October the settings of more than 300 Tor exit relays were altered so that SSH connections through them went to interception servers. According to The Hacker News, anyone who logged in to SSH over Tor with a password between 1 and 5 October after accepting an unfamiliar or changed host key should treat that password as stolen. The relays were gone from Tor's list of usable relays by 01:00 on 6 October Taipei time, and according to the person who found them, encrypted web traffic was passed on as usual.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 10 sources, including Tor Project, tor-relays, kaba.cx

In early October 2026 the settings of more than 300 Tor exit relays (the last hop, which carries Tor traffic to its destination) were altered, and SSH connections (the protocol used to log in to and manage servers remotely) passing through them were sent to interception servers. Users who accepted a fake host key (the key a server uses to prove its identity) and typed a password had it captured. People logging in over SSH through Tor were affected, and people fetching mail over unencrypted connections through Tor may have been too. The relays were gone from Tor's list of usable relays by 01:00 on 6 October Taipei time, and according to the person who found them, encrypted web traffic was passed on as usual.

The finder, a user connecting to SSH over Tor, saw a changed-host-key warning on 2 October. They then scanned all of the roughly 3,000 exits and found 333 that either presented a fake host key or forwarded connections to interception servers, and reported it to the Tor Project that night. Around a dozen presented a fake host key themselves, and over 300 forwarded SSH to the same 12 interception servers.

According to the finder's write-up, once a user went on to log in, the interception server took the password and relayed the session to the real server, so every command typed passed through it. It then logged in to the server the user had meant to reach with the same password and tried to install Ebury, a backdoor that lets attackers log in again later; the finder did not see the installation complete. Ebury sits inside OpenSSH, the server's SSH software, and records the credentials typed at login. ESET's 2024 report counts about 400,000 servers compromised since 2009.

The Tor Network Health team, which monitors the network, posted a notice at 17:50 UTC on 5 October (01:50 on 6 October Taipei time) saying the attacker had gained access to Linux hosts and edited Tor's configuration, even turning non-exits into exits. From the evening of 4 October UTC (early on 5 October Taipei time), the Tor directory authorities (the servers that publish the list of usable relays, known as the consensus) began flagging the affected relays as unusable as exits.

A relay operator comparing public directory data found 377 relays from 59 operators that adopted the same exit policy, the setting that says which ports a relay will connect to, between 1 and 4 October. The analyst notes that this is a settings match and proves neither that every host was compromised nor that every relay intercepted SSH. At the peak these relays held about 7% of usable exit weight (the share of traffic the directory assigns each exit), and since clients pick exits roughly by weight, we estimate a Tor connection had about a 7% chance of using one.

277 of them belonged to one relay family (a set of relays one operator declares together). The family's operator wrote in a post-mortem that server logins, admin rights (sudo) and backups shared one password, and that the management server accepted password logins. How the attackers first got that password is not known. Ebury was found on the two servers the operator examined, and the public data does not show whether other affected hosts carry it.

Perspective

Tor only encrypts traffic inside its own network, so an exit relay can read what is sent to the destination. HTTPS and SSH carry their own encryption and authentication; unencrypted mail protocols do not.

SSH uses the host key to confirm that the server is the real one. Per the OpenSSH manual pages, when a host key changes ssh shows a warning, disables password authentication and, under the default settings, refuses to connect. A password prompt only appears after the user deletes the old key record themselves. A server contacted for the first time has no record to compare against, so the user only sees the usual prompt, and accepting it means accepting the interception server's key.

The Hacker News infers from the SSH specification that only password logins had credentials taken. With a key login (proving identity with a private key on your own computer, without sending a password to the server), each proof is valid only for that session, so the interceptor cannot reuse it against the real server. The report also notes that the interceptor could still accept a key login and show a fake command line. Our inference is that a sudo or other admin password typed there could leak too.

The Hacker News advises anyone who logged in with a password over Tor between 1 and 5 October after accepting an unfamiliar or changed host key to treat that password as stolen. The family's servers had unexplained hidden processes from 30 September, and the operator cannot tell whether those were intercepting SSH too, so earlier logins cannot be ruled out.

The family's operator warns that Ebury records any password typed on an infected server. Checks should be done with a key login or by booting a rescue system, a maintenance environment that does not start the original system.

Other services that used the exposed password can be changed first, and the server that was logged in to after it has been checked. ESET's detection script runs on the server's command line, and only the update merged on 9 October detects this Ebury version; a clean result is no guarantee.

For future administration over Tor, the finder recommends key-based logins. On first connection, the host key fingerprint (a string identifying the key, shown when connecting) can be checked against one obtained from the administrator.

Another option is running SSH as an onion service (a service reachable only through Tor, whose connections never leave the Tor network), which avoids exit relays and so cannot be intercepted by one. The cost is that a private key has to be kept safe and set up again after changing or losing a computer. An onion service needs tor running on the server, one more step than exposing SSH directly.

According to the analyst, most affected relays closed the encrypted mail ports and left the unencrypted ones open, so mail fetched through them travelled in plaintext. No source confirms that mail was actually read, but anyone fetching mail over Tor should still check that their client uses an encrypted connection.

Tor relays are run by volunteers and anyone can join, so finding compromised or malicious relays relies on the Network Health team's scans and user reports. From the finder's report on 2 October to the last affected relay leaving the consensus at 17:00 UTC on 5 October took about three days.

Clients choose exits without regard to where the user is, so a relay's country says nothing about whether a reader was exposed. We, a community based in Taiwan, matched the 377 relays against geolocation data: none was in Taiwan, Japan, South Korea or Hong Kong, while Singapore had 24, all from the one family (geolocation data may contain errors). Our Tor relay dashboard shows exits in Singapore falling from 34 on 3 October to 9 on 4 October (daily snapshots in UTC), which we take to be the flagging. From 3 to 5 October Taiwan had two or three exits, Japan two or three, South Korea two and Hong Kong seven, none of them affected.

For mainland China, the Tor Project's support page recommends letting Tor Browser's Connection Assist try bridges or Snowflake first, then WebTunnel bridges, since direct connections to Tor are blocked in some countries. A bridge replaces only the first hop, and traffic still leaves through an exit relay, so the same advice applies to anyone connecting through one.

People who only use Tor Browser to visit HTTPS sites, and do not use SSH or fetch mail over Tor, need not change anything. As of 24 October we had found no explanation on the Tor Project's blog, status page or mailing lists of why the other 58 operators' relays adopted the same policy. ESET's Ebury researcher wrote on the relay operators' mailing list that there are most likely other compromised relays still unnoticed. Around 25 November is a good time to check whether the Tor Project has published how these relays were compromised, or found any more.

item.title: Cyber intrusions and disputed information ahead of Taiwan's local elections
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: According to a report Taiwan's National Security Bureau sent to the legislature in October, the bureau collected more than 2.5 million items of disputed information from January to September 2026, about 48% more than a year earlier, and that government networks faced about 2.58 million intrusions a day. The bureau assesses that China is expanding its use of AI to influence the 28 November local elections. How the figures were counted is not explained in the news reports.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 30 sources, including National Security Bureau, Taiwan, Laws & Regulations Database of The Republic of China (Taiwan), Liberty Times

Taiwan's National Security Bureau (NSB) sent a written report to the Legislative Yuan on 20 October, and the Liberty Times and Reuters both reported its figures. From January to September 2026, NSB intelligence teams tracking anomalous accounts (social media accounts the bureau considers not controlled by real people, defined in the Perspective below) collected more than 2.5 million items of disputed information, up about 48% from more than 1.69 million a year earlier. According to the Central News Agency, the Government Service Network (GSN), which links government agencies, faced an average of about 2.58 million intrusions a day as of September, with an upward trend since June.

The NSB assesses that China is expanding its use of AI for information manipulation, with the aim of influencing the 28 November local elections. AFP, in a story carried by Hong Kong Free Press, also quoted the report as saying that China's cyber forces use AI agents to scan government websites for vulnerabilities. As of 24 October, we, a community based in Taiwan, found only links to media coverage on the NSB website and not the report itself, so all the figures come from news reports.

The Liberty Times lists Facebook, online forums, Threads and YouTube as the main platforms. Facebook's share rose from 43.6% in the same period of 2025 to 68.9%, and Threads' from 4.5% to 9%. According to the NSB report as relayed by the Liberty Times, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) mostly has official bodies or state media set the narrative frame, then spreads it through proxy accounts, paid commenters and public relations firms, using content farms, fake websites and AI-generated audio and video.

The NSB director appeared before the legislature's Foreign Affairs and National Defense Committee on 22 October, and the Central News Agency reported six forms of election interference the bureau has identified. They are illicit funding, hosting supporters on trips to China, offering cheap flights so that Taiwanese people living in China can return to vote, spreading disinformation, underground election betting, and hacking specific targets to steal election information. The United Daily News reported that the bureau is tracking about 100 cases.

Perspective

The 2.58 million figure counts "intrusions" (侵擾) on the Government Service Network. How the NSB counts a single intrusion is not explained in any of the reports. The Taipei Times rendered it as cyberintrusion attempts. AFP wrote that Taiwan faced 2.6 million cyberattacks a day, widening the scope to the whole of Taiwan and turning intrusions into attacks.

A separate NSB report in January counted nine categories of critical infrastructure and gave about 2.63 million a day on average for 2025. The two reports cover different scopes, so their figures cannot be compared as an increase or decrease.

The 2.5 million figure is the number of items collected by tracking anomalous accounts. The NSB's term is "disputed information" (爭議訊息), which AFP translated as disinformation disseminated by the CCP. In its January report the NSB defined anomalous accounts as social media accounts not controlled by real users, for example accounts with no personal posts, no social interaction, or a foreign persona posting in Chinese. Whether the October report uses the same definition, and whether the platform shares are counted by items or by accounts, is not explained in any of the reports.

As of 24 October, the report does not appear in the transcript of the 21 October press conference of China's Taiwan Affairs Office of the State Council (TAO). Reuters reported that the TAO did not immediately respond, and noted that Beijing has previously denied interfering in Taiwan's elections or spreading disinformation.

A TAO spokesperson has answered two other questions related to election interference and cyberattacks. At the August press conference, a reporter asked about letters Taiwanese prosecutors' offices sent to village and borough chiefs about election investigations, which mentioned "mainland interference in elections". The spokesperson replied that the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) slanders the mainland with claims of election interference every time there is an election, for political gain. In September, asked about the Information, Communications and Electronic Force Command of Taiwan's Ministry of National Defense, the spokesperson said the DPP authorities direct the command to frequently attack mainland network infrastructure.

The Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI) analysed Taiwan's 2024 presidential election and observed at least two China-originated threat actors seeking to interfere. Its assessment was that these operations likely had a minimal impact on the integrity of the election results due to the resilience of Taiwan's civil society. According to Radio Free Asia, Doublethink Lab, a Taiwanese civil society group, concluded in its research on the 2024 election that AI-generated material does not by itself establish who created it, and that attribution depends on account networks and posting behaviour.

Under Taiwan's Civil Servants Election and Recall Act (last amended on 1 July 2026, according to the Laws & Regulations Database), prospective candidates and candidates who find deepfake audio or video of themselves between the election announcement and the day before voting can apply to the police for forensic examination at their own expense. In the act, a deepfake is a false depiction of the person's words or actions made by computer synthesis or other technical means. Once the person has the result and submits a request, platforms must restrict access to or remove the content within two days. Spreading false content through a candidate's deepfake with intent to influence the election, where it is capable of harming the public or others, carries up to seven years' imprisonment.

According to a commentary in Tech Policy Press, as of May 2026 no takedown request had been filed with platforms under this provision. Such requests must also be copied to the election commission running the election, and the commentary's author confirmed the zero count with the Central Election Commission (CEC). The author attributes it to the narrow set of protected people and the narrow time window, a deepfake definition that is hard to apply, and the jurisdictional gap with platforms based overseas.

The Ministry of Digital Affairs (MODA) built an election AI deepfake reporting site under the act to help candidates notify platforms. The United Daily News reported on 10 August that it was expected to go live on 25 August, and MODA's statement stressed that the existing legal procedures and responsibilities remain unchanged. In another report on 20 August, the CEC's director of legal affairs explained that most platform operators are overseas and the site makes it easier for candidates to reach them.

In the 10 August report, a Kuomintang (KMT) legislator argued that the CEC is the authority in charge of elections. The legislator questioned whether MODA was expanding its remit and letting the government decide what information gets taken down, and the Taiwan People's Party caucus convener also worried that content unfavourable to the ruling party could be removed as deepfakes. A DPP legislator said the key is whether the content causes harm to the person depicted.

South Korea, Singapore and Japan regulate election deepfakes differently. Under South Korea's Public Official Election Act, as amended on 28 December 2023, no one may produce, edit, distribute, screen or post AI-made virtual sound, images or video that are hard to distinguish from reality for election campaigning, from 90 days before election day through election day. The amendment took effect one month after promulgation, which we calculate as 29 January 2024, since its supplementary provisions give no date. A violation carries up to seven years' imprisonment or a fine of 10 million to 50 million won.

Outside that 90-day window, such content used for campaigning must be labelled as AI-made under National Election Commission rules, and failing to label, on its own, carries an administrative fine of up to 10 million won. We have not looked at enforcement figures.

Singapore's Elections (Integrity of Online Advertising) (Amendment) Act 2024 took effect on 22 January 2025 and amended the Parliamentary Elections Act and the Presidential Elections Act. It is now an offence to publish online election advertising during the election period that realistically depicts a candidate saying or doing something they did not, where the depiction was generated or manipulated by digital means and the publisher knows or ought reasonably to have known that the content is election advertising. The penalty is a fine of up to S$1,000, up to 12 months' imprisonment, or both, and it is a defence to prove that the publisher did not know and had no reason to believe that the candidate had not said or done it.

According to the government's press release on the bill, the ban also covers non-AI techniques such as Photoshop editing, dubbing and splicing, and runs from the issue of the writ of election to the close of polling. We could not find a statutory definition of election period, so that timing relies on the press release. According to the same press release, the Returning Officer can also direct publishers, social media services and internet access providers to take down such content or disable access for users in Singapore. Under the amendment act, a social media service that fails to comply with a direction faces a fine of up to S$1 million, and candidates can ask the Returning Officer to give a direction.

Japan's current Public Offices Election Act has no deepfake-specific provision, and we found no match for terms such as artificial intelligence or deepfake in the current text. The nearest provision makes publishing false matters about a candidate to stop them being elected punishable by up to four years' imprisonment or a fine of up to 1 million yen.

An amendment promulgated on 17 July 2026 takes effect on 1 March 2027 and applies to elections announced from that date. Under it, anyone posting online campaign material with AI-made or AI-altered images or video must make that clear on the recipient's screen, except for minor alterations or images unlikely to be mistaken for real footage. Internet users also have a duty not to publish false matters about candidates so as to harm the fairness of elections, though in the amended text on e-Gov no penalty clause refers to either duty. Large platforms must also take measures to reduce the harm of information that threatens the fairness of elections.

Read against these laws, our view is that Taiwan's deepfake takedown route starts only when a candidate asks for forensic examination, while South Korea bans the use of AI-made content of this kind for campaigning in the 90 days before an election and Singapore lets an election official order removal. Japan's labelling duty will not apply until elections announced from March 2027.

Readers in Taiwan who see a suspicious election message on Facebook, Threads or a LINE group can submit it through the complaints section of the Taiwan FactCheck Center website, or add MyGoPen on LINE by searching for @mygopen and forward it for checking. MyGoPen offers only one-to-one checking and does not handle personal subjective claims. According to the Taichung District Prosecutors Office, as reported by the United Daily News in May, disinformation and foreign interference in elections can be reported by calling 0800-024-099 and pressing 4, and the reporter's identity is kept confidential by law. The Hsinchu District Prosecutors Office lists the same hotline.

The deepfake forensic and takedown procedure under Taiwan's election act is open only to prospective candidates and candidates, and does not apply when an ordinary member of the public is impersonated.

A few questions can help readers weigh the claims made before the vote. First, whether outsiders can see what the NSB's figures and the TAO's counter-accusations are based on, and whether independent research can verify the attribution. Second, whether security and law enforcement agencies can trace foreign money and manipulation before the vote, and whether investigation results are published afterwards. Third, how deepfake takedown rules, in Taiwan and elsewhere, trade off reducing disinformation against protecting speech.

item.title: Disputed matching of protest footage by Baden-Württemberg police and Berlin's behaviour-recognition cameras
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: According to court testimony reported by netzpolitik.org, an officer at the State Criminal Police Office of Baden-Württemberg in Germany ran footage of a registered demonstration through a computer after the event and identified four participants who, to date, have no connection to the case. In October, Berlin police began testing cameras that analyse behaviour at high-crime locations, and the police law rules out automated facial recognition on that footage. The EU AI Act in principle prohibits real-time identification by law enforcement in publicly accessible spaces, while post-event identification is classed as high-risk and becomes subject to authorisation and other rules from December 2027.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 32 sources, including netzpolitik.org, Polizei Berlin, Gesetz- und Verordnungsblatt für Berlin

An officer of the State Criminal Police Office (LKA) of Baden-Württemberg in Germany testified in a criminal case before the Stuttgart Regional Court. netzpolitik.org's report of 21 October drew on a Stuttgart weekly's coverage of the hearing and on statements from a defence lawyer for the accused.

The officer said that, to check whether two of the accused had already come to police attention, he had analysed footage of a registered demonstration in Ulm. Besides the two accused, the matching identified four other participants who, to date, have no connection to the case. The report's headline and subheading refer to facial recognition, but the officer's testimony did not say which system was used. He said he had followed a "principle of completeness" and checked whom else the computer could recognise, and the report gives no source for this principle.

According to the report, the witness did not answer in court who ordered the matching or on what legal basis. In its reply to netzpolitik.org, the LKA stated that it could not comment on ongoing proceedings and that personal data is collected in line with the relevant legal provisions, and it did not respond to the question about the "principle of completeness". A lawyer at the German civil rights group Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte (GFF, Society for Civil Rights) argued that no such principle allows the police to identify everyone who has ever demonstrated alongside a suspect. Without concrete indications that these people were accomplices, the lawyer considers such investigative measures unlawful.

The report does not name the system the officer used. Its background section covers the facial recognition system of Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), with no statement that it was the one used in this case. The system has run since 2008 and compares surveillance camera images or wanted-person photos with photos in INPOL, the police database. Figures cited in the same report put INPOL at about 7.6 million photos of some 5.4 million people in January 2026, with federal and state criminal police offices running about 313,500 searches in 2025.

Since 6 October, Berlin police have been testing a different kind of camera at Kottbusser Tor, an area the city's interior department lists as a high-crime location. According to the police explainer page, the system recognises situations and does not analyse faces or personal characteristics. Administrative rules published in October by the Senate Department for the Interior and Sport (Senatsverwaltung für Inneres und Sport) give beating, kicking and people lying on the ground or falling as example situations. During the test phase the system neither detects nor raises alerts, but footage is stored.

According to the department's answer in September, the round-the-clock phase is expected to start in the fourth quarter of 2026.

Under Berlin's General Security and Public Order Act (ASOG), amended in December 2025, automated remote biometric identification on footage from the high-crime-location cameras is ruled out, as is using that footage to test or train remote biometric identification programs. Remote biometric identification means recognising a person from a distance, without their involvement, by matching features such as the face. Under the same amendment, police may separately, with a court order, match face and voice data of specific people after the fact against personal data publicly available on the internet.

According to the police page, the system is switched off during assemblies whenever participants might be caught on camera. Footage from the test phase onwards is kept for 28 days.

Perspective

Real-time identification matches and recognises people while they are being filmed, and post-event identification runs the matching on footage already recorded. The Ulm case involved post-event matching, and according to official descriptions Berlin's system does neither and only assesses what is happening in the frame.

The EU's Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) has different rules for the two. Under Article 5, in force since February 2025, real-time identification by law enforcement in publicly accessible spaces is prohibited, with three exceptions.

The three are searching for victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings and sexual exploitation and for missing persons, preventing a specific and imminent threat to life or a terrorist attack, and locating suspects of serious crimes. Each must be strictly necessary, and member states must expressly allow it in national law. Each use requires prior authorisation from a court or an independent authority, and in urgent cases the request must follow within 24 hours at the latest.

Post-event identification falls outside the prohibition and is classed as high-risk to the extent its use is permitted under EU or national law (going by the wording of Annex III, our reading is that the AI Act itself does not authorise such use). Under Article 26(10), an investigation targeting a specific suspect requires an authorisation request in advance or within 48 hours at the latest, except for the initial identification of a potential suspect based on facts directly linked to the offence. Untargeted use with no link to a criminal offence, criminal proceedings, a genuine threat or the search for a specific missing person is also banned.

These high-risk rules were originally due to apply in August 2026, and under a simplification amendment (the AI Omnibus) in force since July 2026 they now apply from December 2027.

The Ulm case involved post-event matching on footage already recorded, but with the system unknown, it cannot be confirmed whether it counts as remote biometric identification as the AI Act defines it. The Act's authorisation rules did not yet apply at the time, so legality turns on German national law, which is exactly what GFF questions. According to the police page, Berlin's system recognises situations, not identities. In June, Berlin police's chief digital officer told a parliamentary committee that, by the force's own assessment, the system would probably count as low-risk under the AI Act.

The European Commission's 2025 guidelines on prohibited practices include an example in which police pull footage from street CCTV and use post-event facial recognition to match it against social media photos to find the organiser of a protest. The guidelines' assessment is that this use is not prohibited and counts as high-risk. According to a footnote, it is questionable whether post-event identification is strictly necessary to identify the protester.

The example is drawn from a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights. In that case the court held that, with no risk to public order or transport safety, both post-event and live use of facial recognition were disproportionate. The guidelines themselves are not legally binding.

Identification and anonymisation are one point of contention in Berlin. In an interview on 22 September, Berlin's data protection commissioner said that the law rules out automated biometric identification but does not prevent a specific person being identified manually, case by case, from stored footage. Manually building profiles of movements and social contacts within the monitored area also remains technically possible.

At a hearing of the Berlin parliament's interior committee in June, an expert from the German hacker collective Chaos Computer Club (CCC) argued that stick-figure images do not count as anonymisation, since timestamps alone link them back to the original footage. At the same session, the senator responsible for the interior (Innensenator) said that the system carries out no biometric or other automated matching of personal data. The senator also said it would not be expanded into citywide surveillance, and according to the administrative rules, the vector data the system produces cannot be reconstructed into images.

Effectiveness is the other point of contention, and in its September answer the interior department sets the system's goal as early detection of violence and of people on the ground who need help. A researcher who studied the Hamburg pilot told the June hearing that situations police officers mentioned in interviews as triggering alerts included hugs, children kicking footballs, people pushing prams and people lying on the ground (Hamburg uses software developed by a different institution). The researcher said that researchers have no precise information on how many false alarms occur at each site, or what they are. Hamburg police have published one figure, which the researcher considers unreliable.

As of its 6 September answer, the city government had no plans to commission an external academic evaluation.

Berlin held a state election on 20 September, and according to netzpolitik.org, the exploratory paper of the SPD, the Greens and the Left Party (the preliminary document drawn up before coalition talks) includes an evaluation of video surveillance in 2028. The three parties can begin negotiations only after the Left Party votes at its party conference on 31 October. In August, the Greens' and the Left Party's parliamentary groups asked Berlin's Constitutional Court to review the police law, including the behaviour-recognition cameras. They did not seek a suspension, so the law remains in force until a ruling.

In a coalition agreement published in May 2026, the Greens and the CDU in Baden-Württemberg pledged to expand the Mannheim model, on the grounds that AI video surveillance can serve both security and fundamental rights. Mannheim has piloted behaviour-recognition cameras for hitting, kicking and similar acts since 2018, and the agreement includes adding remote biometric identification at the pilot sites, without saying whether real-time or post-event. According to netzpolitik.org's report in May, this would require amending the state police law. As of 24 October, we had found no record of such an amendment.

According to the same May report, Frankfurt was at the time the only place in Germany using real-time facial recognition on public cameras, and in April netzpolitik.org reported that each search needs a judge's order.

People who spend time near Berlin's pilot sites can tell from signs where these cameras are. Under ASOG, police must put up signs and publish the locations, and the administrative rules list four pilot sites. The cameras are switched off during assemblies, but footage of people passing at other times is kept for 28 days and may be viewed manually during that period. For people who join protests, even away from Berlin's pilot sites, post-event matching of existing footage like that in the Ulm case is currently governed by German national law.

Under Article 9 of Taiwan's Police Power Exercise Act, when facts give sufficient grounds to believe that the conduct of participants in an assembly, parade or other public event may endanger public safety or order, police may photograph, record or use other technical means to collect participants' on-site activity data during the event, extending to third parties where unavoidable. The police make that judgement on the facts, and the article does not require court authorisation. Data must be destroyed when the event ends unless it needs to be kept to investigate a crime or other violation, and retained data must be destroyed within one year of its creation at the latest, except in cases indicted and still on trial or concerning violations of the Organized Crime Prevention Act.

We, a community based in Taiwan, found no law that expressly regulates police use of facial recognition matching. Neither the Police Power Exercise Act nor the Personal Data Protection Act, the two laws we searched, contains any reference to faces or biometric features, and we did not read the National Police Agency's internal rules.

In Japan, police register photos of arrested suspects in a database managed by the National Police Agency, following the National Public Safety Commission's Rules on the Management and Use of Suspect Photographs, under which the photos are kept to assist criminal investigations; the rules make no mention of facial recognition or matching. Answering questions in the Cabinet Committees of the House of Representatives in March 2021 and the House of Councillors in May 2021, police officials explained that when police obtain a suspect's facial image from security cameras in an individual case, for example with the cooperation of the camera's operator under the Code of Criminal Procedure, they match it against suspect photos held by the police to help identify the suspect. In the March answer, the official put the police's suspect photo data at about 11.7 million items at the end of 2020, including people whose acquittals had become final, and said keeping those photos posed no legal problem, while photos from wrongful arrests are deleted. We found no law or National Public Safety Commission rule that expressly regulates this matching, and we did not look into rules on police filming at assemblies in Japan.

In South Korea, we found no statute specifically on police filming at assemblies, and the practice rests on the National Police Agency's internal Rules on Evidence-Gathering Activities at Assemblies. Under the rules, filming for criminal investigation is generally limited to while or just after a violent or other crime is committed (or shortly before, when harm to others is imminent and evidence urgently needs to be secured), to the minimum extent necessary, and the people being filmed must be notified in advance. Footage not needed for an investigation must be deleted as soon as the assembly ends, footage may be entered into an evidence-reading program to confirm suspects' identities, and footage of unidentified people still needed for an investigation may be kept until the limitation period for the offence expires.

Under the Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and the Establishment of Trust, in force since 22 January 2026, AI systems that may significantly affect life, bodily safety or fundamental rights and are used to analyse biometric data such as faces for criminal investigations or arrests are classed as high-impact AI. AI businesses that provide them owe risk management, explanation, user protection, human oversight and record-keeping duties, and the act defines AI businesses as those that develop and provide AI or provide products or services using it, state agencies included. We found no dedicated law or police guideline on facial recognition matching in South Korea, and we did not check whether police have applied the new act in practice, or whether police using such a system count as an AI business under the act.

Readers can compare rules across places with a few questions. First, whether the law covers real-time identification, post-event identification or both. Second, whether matching needs prior authorisation from a court or an independent authority, and how data on people unconnected to a case who appear on camera is handled. Third, whether governments publish the number of uses and error rates so that outsiders can assess how well the systems work.

item.title: Lawsuit and criminal investigations over Telenor's Myanmar user data
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Telenor's Myanmar subsidiary handed user data to the military after the 2021 coup, and its Norwegian parent now faces a class action, which a court allowed to proceed on 17 September. Norwegian police have also opened two criminal investigations into the parent company. According to Telenor, local law required it to provide the data, and employees who refused risked imprisonment, torture or the death penalty. The case also raises how user data and surveillance equipment are handled when a telecom operator leaves a country.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 23 sources, including Open Society Justice Initiative, SOMO, Politiet

Telenor's Myanmar subsidiary handed user data to the military after the February 2021 coup, and its Norwegian parent, Telenor ASA, now faces a class action over it. On 8 April, the Swedish non-profit Justice and Accountability Initiative (JAI) filed the suit at Asker and Bærum District Court in Norway on behalf of Myanmar customers whose data was handed over, seeking EUR 9,000 for each of them. On 17 September the court rejected Telenor's procedural objection and allowed the case to proceed as a class action, a ruling that does not yet decide whether Telenor is liable. Norwegian police have separately opened two criminal investigations into Telenor ASA, about 54% of which is owned by the Norwegian state.

According to a press release from the Open Society Justice Initiative (OSJI), another organisation backing the suit, the military frequently demanded data on specific users from Telenor's Myanmar subsidiary after the coup, and the plaintiffs know of at least 1,253 numbers whose data was handed over. The plaintiffs claim that Telenor ASA is liable because it either failed to prevent the disclosures or authorised its subsidiary to make them despite knowing the risks. According to SOMO, a Dutch research centre on multinational corporations that also supports the suit, the class action is opt-out, so every customer whose data was handed over is covered by the claim unless they actively withdraw.

Norwegian police announced the two investigations on 15 September, naming Telenor ASA as a suspect in both. The National Criminal Investigation Service (Kripos) is investigating suspected complicity in crimes against humanity for the period from the coup to the completion of the sale on 25 March 2022, during which the subsidiary repeatedly handed customers' historical traffic data to the military. The Norwegian Police Security Service (PST) is investigating whether sanctioned surveillance equipment was transferred with the sale without a permit from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. According to Telenor's press release, no individuals have been named as suspects.

As of 23 October, we had found no report that either investigation had led to an indictment.

Telenor announced in July 2021 that it would sell its Myanmar business to M1 Group for USD 105 million, and the sale was completed on 25 March 2022. Telenor's announcement of September 2021 said that staying would have required activating intercept equipment for use by the Myanmar authorities, meaning systems that let the authorities monitor communications. That equipment is subject to Norwegian and international sanctions, and the announcement said activating it was unacceptable for Telenor. A Telenor article from February 2022 said the law required traffic data to be retained and staff could not be told to delete it, which left no good alternative to a sale.

Perspective

According to Telenor's 2021 explanation, the call records an operator keeps by law cover both parties, the time, the duration and the base station the call went through, but not the content of the call. Our inference is that the fields Telenor listed are enough on their own to show who a person is in contact with and roughly where they are, without anyone hearing a call.

Telenor's press release says employees who refused the military's orders risked imprisonment, torture or the death penalty, and that the company had no real choice. Telenor's page on the lawsuit also says the company sees no basis for liability, because the data had to be provided under local law. In OSJI's press release, the plaintiffs' lawyer says they hold evidence of cases where the team at headquarters expressly recommended handing over data, and that the filings include several requests that were escalated to the risk assessment team at Telenor's head office in Norway.

The National Contact Point (NCP) that the Norwegian government set up under the guidelines of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) handles complaints about corporate conduct, but it is not a judicial body and cannot order compensation. In 2021, 474 civil society organisations in Myanmar filed a complaint through SOMO over the way Telenor left Myanmar.

The conclusion of the NCP's final statement of December 2025 is that Telenor identified and mitigated some serious risks when it left, and that protecting employees' lives and safety is central to a company's responsibility to respect human rights. The same statement also says that systematically giving priority to one group of rights-holders, the employees, did not meet the expectations of the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises on Responsible Business Conduct. Telenor's response said it disagreed with this conclusion.

The same response accepts that companies should plan a responsible exit before entering volatile markets, but notes that this became a formal part of international human rights frameworks only in 2022 and 2023. The NCP concluded that if Telenor's due diligence on entering Myanmar had already covered the most severe risks, such as a forced exit, Telenor would most likely have had more ability to reduce risk than it actually had. The NCP did not decide whether the guidelines strictly require an exit strategy at entry.

On what was transferred, Telenor's position is that local law required the data to be retained and not deleted. Telenor's page on the case also says its Myanmar subsidiary did not activate the intercept equipment, and that after the coup it was forced to stop disclosing the scope of government requests. Telenor's statements concern activation, while the police press release does not say whether the surveillance equipment in the PST investigation is this same equipment. The NCP concluded that Telenor should have carried out a new risk assessment once the Myanmar authorities required the buyer to find a local partner as majority owner.

An analysis by Ranking Digital Rights, which rates the human rights performance of technology companies, says interception systems should not be transferred in a sale as ordinary equipment, and that the Myanmar buyer stopped all transparency reporting after renaming itself ATOM Myanmar. A 2023 document from the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) says companies selling operations should consider the human rights commitments of potential buyers and guide the sale to more responsible ones.

We are a community based in Taiwan, where the Telecommunications Management Act requires carriers to keep communication records for a set period and keep them confidential, and to assist with interception and with requests for communication records and user information under the Communication Security and Surveillance Act. Subscribers in Taiwan can ask their carrier for their own communication and billing records, which the carrier must provide, but the records stay with the carrier and authorities can still obtain them under the law. Chunghwa Telecom, Far EasTone and Taiwan Mobile publish counts of government requests in their sustainability reports or ESG pages: 247,032 at Chunghwa Telecom and 253,731 at Far EasTone in 2025, and 270,578 at Taiwan Mobile in 2024. The three differ in year, unit and method, and Chunghwa Telecom changed its method from 2025, so the figures cannot be compared directly.

In Taiwan, a carrier that holds spectrum or a quarter of a market needs approval from the National Communications Commission (NCC) to transfer all or most of its business, and the factors the NCC weighs include users' rights and national security, though the Telecommunications Management Act does not say how subscriber data is transferred. Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act has no provision on transfers in a merger or sale, as far as we found in the statute text. In South Korea and Japan, the transfer rules we found are in general data protection law, which applies to all businesses, and we did not check telecom-specific rules or whether these rules, written for business transfers, mergers and succession, cover a sale of 100% of the shares in a subsidiary like Telenor's.

South Korea's Personal Information Protection Act requires advance notice, including how to object, when personal data moves because a business is transferred or merged, and the recipient may use the data only for the original purposes. Under Japan's Act on the Protection of Personal Information, a successor in a merger or other business succession is not treated as a third party, so the consent rule for passing data to third parties does not apply. The successor may not use the data beyond the original purposes without consent. The two Japanese provisions we checked contain no notice requirement, and we did not review the rest of Japan's act or the guidelines of its Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC).

Myanmar customers whose data was handed over are included in the class action by default and must actively opt out if they want to leave it. Other readers do not need to do anything.

The case can be weighed against each side's standards through three questions. First, whether the parent company is responsible for its subsidiary handing over data, where Telenor's position is that the data had to be provided under local law and the plaintiffs claim the parent authorised it knowing the risks. Second, how an operator facing government demands should weigh its responsibility to protect employees against its responsibility to protect users. Third, what leaving and staying each cost, and whether user data and surveillance equipment should go with a sale, where Telenor's position is that local law required the data to be retained and not deleted.

According to SOMO and OSJI, Telenor had one month to appeal the 17 September ruling, until about 17 October. As of 23 October, we had found no report of an appeal. Readers can watch for the court's hearing date and for whether either investigation leads to an indictment.
